Is the Galaxy S27 Ultra really going to be a significant downgrade for Samsung fans? It could be, at least when it comes to its cameras.

Industry observers note that earlier this month, Mashable reported on recent leaks suggesting that the Samsung Galaxy S27 lineup wasn't going to get much of an upgrade compared to its predecessors. The Samsung Galaxy S27 Ultra fared slightly better than the other models, according to the leaks. It appears the Samsung Galaxy S27 Ultra will get a main camera sensor upgrade, along with a better selfie camera and a 5x zoom lens.

However, upcoming leaks suggest the device could also lose a few camera features.

The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

According to recent reports, according to leaker Ice Universe, Samsung may be dropping the laser autofocus module from the Galaxy S27 Ultra. Laser autofocus, also known as laser AF, uses a dedicated sensor that helps the camera rapidly lock focus on a subject. If the leak is accurate, the S27 Ultra would be the first Galaxy S Ultra model without laser autofocus since at least 2021, when Samsung released the Galaxy S21 Ultra.

The removal of laser autofocus appears to be connected to the latest camera layout on the Galaxy S27 Ultra, which was also previously leaked by Ice Universe. The Galaxy S27 Ultra will reportedly move away from the vertical camera setup on the Galaxy S26 Ultra and have a horizontal camera bar instead. The new layout is reportedly the reason behind the removal of laser autofocus.

According to recent reports, that's not the only potential downgrade, as PhoneArena points out. Other leaks have also pointed to the Galaxy S27 Ultra losing its 3x telephoto lens.

If these leaks pan out, will the Galaxy S27 Ultra have other newly introduced features to balance out the downgrades and still lure in current owners looking to upgrade? We'll likely find out at Samsung Galaxy Unpacked early next year.

#105435. Industry News: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1403 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1403 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that about 2,000 years ago, the remnants of a massive ice sheet in the Canadian Arctic began expanding once again.
  • The findings suggest that global warming may have interrupted a new ice age that was already getting underway, fundamentally altering a natural climate cycle that has shaped Earth for millions of years.
  • "It was just getting started, everything was normal, the next glaciation was about to happen -- and yet it stopped," claims Nicolás Young, a geochemist at Columbia Climate School's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that about 2,000 years ago, the remnants of a massive ice sheet in the Canadian Arctic began expanding once again. According to new research, this slow buildup of ice may have marked the beginning of Earth's next glacial period, commonly called an ice age. But something unexpected happened. By the 1960s, rising summer temperatures had reversed the trend, causing the ice to retreat instead of grow.

The findings suggest that global warming may have interrupted a new ice age that was already getting underway, fundamentally altering a natural climate cycle that has shaped Earth for millions of years.

"It was just getting started, everything was normal, the next glaciation was about to happen -- and yet it stopped," claims Nicolás Young, a geochemist at Columbia Climate School's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. "It's a very powerful example of how we have jolted the system.".

Ancient Arctic Ice Reveals a Surprising Climate History.

In a study published in Science, Young and fellow Lamont geochemist Joerg Schaefer, along with their colleagues, investigated the history of the Laurentide Ice Sheet. This enormous mass of ice covered much of Canada and the northern United States between approximately 95,000 and 20,000 years ago.

It has been revealed that at its greatest extent, the Laurentide stretched from north of the Arctic Circle all the way south to Illinois. In some locations, its ice was more than two miles thick. Although most of this enormous ice sheet disappeared as the climate warmed, one surviving piece remains.

Known as the Barnes Ice Cap, this ancient remnant sits on central Baffin Island in Nunavut, Canada, and covers an area roughly the size of Delaware.

"People always say that it disappeared, but that's not true," indicates Young.

Scientists already knew that the Laurentide Ice Sheet had repeatedly grown and retreated during the roughly 2.6 million years since extensive continental glaciation began in North America. What remained uncertain was whether the ice sheet had ever become smaller than it is today before expanding again.

Answering that question could reveal whether a new cycle of glaciation had begun much more recently than scientists previously believed.

(A note on terminology: Technically, we are still living in an ice age-the Late Cenozoic Ice Age-which started about 34 million years ago. Within it, colder glacial periods alternate with warmer interglacial ones, including the one we live in now. What people casually call an "ice age" is usually a glacial period. The last glacial period ended about 11,700 years ago.).

Ancient Plants Preserved Beneath Ice Hold the Clues.

Industry observers note that piecing together the history of an ice sheet is particularly challenging when researchers are looking for evidence of its smallest extent and earliest stages of regrowth. As glaciers advance, they frequently scrape across the land, destroying the geological traces that could reveal where and when the ice first began spreading.

The Barnes Ice Cap, however, offers an unusual opportunity to investigate this history.

Unlike most glaciers, it is frozen directly to the bedrock beneath it and does not slide across the landscape. As a result, plants that once grew in areas later covered by expanding ice can remain preserved in place for thousands of years.

Since the Barnes Ice Cap began retreating in 1960, previously buried vegetation has gradually emerged from beneath the melting ice. Researchers can collect these ancient plant remains and determine when they were alive using radiocarbon dating.

This technique measures carbon-14, a harmlessly radioactive form of carbon that living organisms absorb from the atmosphere. Once an organism dies, its carbon-14 begins breaking down at a predictable rate. By measuring how much remains, scientists can estimate when the plant stopped growing and became buried beneath the ice.

These dates provide a record of when the advancing glacier covered different parts of the landscape.

"If you do this enough times, you can actually develop a timeline of that ice margin systematically advancing over plants. You're actually tracking the expansion of that ice margin," claims Young.

Earth's Next Ice Age May Have Begun 2,000 Years Ago.

The research team examined ancient vegetation uncovered by the retreating Barnes Ice Cap, along with plant remains exposed beneath smaller ice caps that have recently melted in the surrounding region.

Together, these samples allowed the scientists to reconstruct thousands of years of glacial change.

According to recent reports, their results indicate that the Laurentide Ice Sheet reached its smallest extent approximately 3,000 years ago. Then, around 2,000 years ago, temperatures became cold enough for the remaining ice to begin expanding again.

Young and his colleagues argue that this renewed growth should be recognized as the start of Earth's next glacial period.

That interpretation differs from previous research based on climate models, which has generally suggested that the next glaciation would not begin for thousands or even tens of thousands of years.

The disagreement partly comes down to how scientists define the beginning of a glacial period. Rather than waiting until enormous ice sheets have spread across continents, Young's team proposes that the first sustained expansion of an existing ice sheet should mark the starting point.

Under that definition, the next glaciation had already begun long before modern scientists recognized it.

The discovery also casts fresh light on a controversial scientific debate from the 1970s, when some climate researchers suggested that another ice age might be approaching.

"It actually was happening," Young says. "They couldn't quite prove it, but now we sort of have the evidence.".

Recent findings suggest that however, this early expansion would not have produced an immediate or dramatic transformation of the planet. According to Young, it would have taken thousands of years for the cooling to become noticeable and roughly 30,000 years for the Laurentide Ice Sheet to regain its enormous continental dimensions.

The process was only in its earliest stages when the warming climate brought it to a halt.

Global Warming Reversed the Growth of the Ice Sheet.

By the 1960s, conditions had changed enough that the Barnes Ice Cap was losing more ice during the summer than it could replace through winter snowfall.

Instead of continuing to expand, the ancient ice began shrinking.

According to the researchers' interpretation, this reversal effectively ended the developing glacial period before it could progress into a full-scale ice age.

It has been revealed that the consequences may extend far beyond the present day. Models projecting the future of the Barnes Ice Cap indicate that it could disappear entirely within the next few centuries.

"That will be the true very last remains of the Laurentide, disappearing for good," Young states.

The Loss of an Ancient Ice Cap Could Change Future Ice Ages.

The disappearance of the Barnes Ice Cap could also have implications for how future glacial periods develop.

In the past, the Laurentide Ice Sheet provided a starting point for renewed glaciation whenever Earth's climate cooled sufficiently. Because a large existing mass of ice helps create conditions favorable for further ice accumulation, it can trigger reinforcing processes that allow glaciers to expand.

Scientists describe this kind of process as a positive feedback. In this case, existing ice helps promote the growth of additional ice, allowing an ice sheet to become increasingly extensive as temperatures remain cold.

Without the Laurentide's last surviving remnant, a future glacial period might unfold differently.

Recent findings suggest that researchers cannot yet determine when another glaciation could begin under atmospheric conditions influenced by elevated greenhouse gas concentrations. If enormous continental ice sheets eventually start forming again, they may have to develop without the ancient ice that previously helped initiate their growth.

Industry observers note that the findings suggest that global warming has done more than melt glaciers and shrink existing ice sheets. It may have interrupted a glacial cycle that was already beginning, while also removing a feature that helped sustain ice age cycles across North America for millions of years.

"What has been an extremely natural and predictable phenomenon is now gone," notes Young.

Finland's Prime Minister Sanna Marin concedes election

📅 02 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 2 min read (490 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finland’s left-wing Prime Minister Sanna Marin conceded defeat on Sunday in the Nordic country’s parliamentary election as the opposition right-wing National Coalition Party (NCP) claimed victory in a tightly fought contest.
  • The pro-business NCP was expected to win 48 of the 200 seats in parliament, narrowly ahead of the nationalist Finns Party with 46 seats and Marin’s Social Democrats on 43 seats, justice ministry election data demonstrated with all ballots counted.
  • “We got the biggest mandate,” NCP leader Petteri Orpo remarked in a speech to followers, vowing to “fix Finland” and its economy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finland’s left-wing Prime Minister Sanna Marin conceded defeat on Sunday in the Nordic country’s parliamentary election as the opposition right-wing National Coalition Party (NCP) claimed victory in a tightly fought contest.

The pro-business NCP was expected to win 48 of the 200 seats in parliament, narrowly ahead of the nationalist Finns Party with 46 seats and Marin’s Social Democrats on 43 seats, justice ministry election data demonstrated with all ballots counted.

“We got the biggest mandate,” NCP leader Petteri Orpo remarked in a speech to followers, vowing to “fix Finland” and its economy.

He will get the first chance at forming a coalition to obtain majority in parliament as Marin’s era as prime minister was expected to end.

Popular abroad, at home Marin faces battle to keep her job.

“We have gained support, we have gained more seats (in parliament). That’s an excellent achievement, even if we did not finish first today,” the prime minister said in a speech to party members.

Marin, 37, the world’s youngest prime minister when she took office in 2019, is considered by fans around the globe as a millennial role model for progressive upcoming leaders, but at home she has faced criticism for her partying and her government’s public spending.

Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin takes drug test following partying backlash.

While she remains very popular among many Finns, particularly young moderates, she antagonized some conservatives with lavish spending on pensions and education they see as not frugal enough.

The NCP has led in polls for almost two years although its lead had melted away in recent months. It has promised to curb spending and stop the rise of public debt, which has reached just over 70% of GDP since Marin took office in 2019.

Orpo accused Marin of eroding Finland’s economic resilience at a time when Europe’s energy crisis, driven by Russia’s war in Ukraine, has hit the country hard and the cost of living has increased.

Orpo has stated he will negotiate with all groups to obtain a majority in parliament, while Marin has said her Social Democrats may govern with the NCP but will not go into government with the Finns Party.

Marin called the Finns Party “openly racist” during a debate in January – an accusation the nationalist group rejected.

It has been revealed that the Finns Party’s main goal is to reduce what leader Riikka Purra has called “harmful” immigration from developing countries outside the European Union. It also calls for austerity policies to curb deficit spending, a stance it shares with the NCP.

Most notable of Marin’s foreign policy actions has been her push, along with President Sauli Niinisto, for the country to make a watershed policy U-turn by seeking NATO membership in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

That process is now almost complete, with Helsinki expected to join within days after all the Western defense alliance’s 30 members approved the accession.

Thanksgiving Travel Will Be a Stormy Mess

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (859 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that expect travel headaches from coast to coast this week.
  • A very active pattern draped across North America will keep the storm train running in the days ahead.
  • Industry observers note that the stormy setup arrives at the peak travel time of the year in the US.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that expect travel headaches from coast to coast this week. Several rounds of disruptive weather sweep are likely to cause delays at airports and make for challenging driving conditions just in time for the Thanksgiving long weekend.

A very active pattern draped across North America will keep the storm train running in the days ahead. Potent systems rolling into the West Coast will bring disruptions from Seattle to San Francisco, where high tides could swamp airport runways. East of the Rockies, a major coastal storm expected to develop on Wednesday will generate widespread heavy rain and winds so gusty there’s a “significant chance” the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade could be balloonless for the first time in 55 years. The same system will also deliver the season’s first measurable snow in some areas.

Industry observers note that the stormy setup arrives at the peak travel time of the year in the US. The Transportation Security Administration screened 3.1 million passengers to close out the long weekend in 2025, marking the agency’s highest passenger volume on record. And with the extreme weather this week is set to sweep across some of the country’s biggest travel hubs, it could upend the best-laid travel looks.

A persistent series of low-pressure systems will drag waves of heavy precipitation into the Pacific Northwest throughout the week, making delays and the occasional cancellation likely for flyers in Seattle and Portland.

The real risk for delays begins to pile up when rain and gusty winds follow a cold front into northern California on Tuesday night Though the worst of the rain will likely clear out in time for the bulk of Wednesday’s travel, flooding is still a major concern for low-lying highways and parts of San Francisco International Airport.

It has been revealed that forecasters expect a near-record king tide—that is, one of the highest tides of the year—on Tuesday and Wednesday. King tides are a normal occurrence, but this year’s will be exacerbated by record-high sea levels driven by the Super El Niño. The climate phenomenon has pushed warm water toward the coast, which takes up more space than cold water.

Monday’s forecast from the National Weather Service called for a high tide of 8.5 feet at the San Francisco gauge on Wednesday morning, which is just shy of the all-time record of 8.66 feet set in January 1983, another Super El Niño year.

Farther east, the atmospheric ingredients are lining up for a sprawling nor’easter to develop over the Southeast by Wednesday and move north through New England by the end of the week.

Widespread heavy rainfall will accompany the storm northward, potentially worsening highway traffic as commuters and vacationers alike navigate slick roads in gloomy conditions. Gusty winds will reduce visibility during heavy rainfall. Forecasters expect several inches of rain along the East Coast, especially along the Interstate 95 corridor between South Carolina and Latest York.

Airline delays are almost certain given the dreaded mix of precipitation, low clouds, and stiff winds. The greatest impacts are likely in Charlotte and Raleigh in North Carolina on Wednesday, followed by Washington, DC, Philadelphia, New York, and Boston on Thursday.

Sources indicate that all these cities are home to major hubs for various airlines. Foul conditions at one of those airports can have ripple effects that lead to delayed or canceled flights down the line, including in cities where the weather is just fine. This may be the most impactful Thanksgiving weather since a nor’easter rolled up the East Coast on the Wednesday and Thursday of the holiday weekend in 2014. That storm hit the major hubs with high winds and heavy rain, as well as up to a foot of wet snow across much of the interior Northeast. The event led to thousands of cancelled and delayed flights. (The US also got a taste of travel trouble earlier this month when a Federal Aviation Administration ground stop left travelers stranded.).

The conditions could get so dire, that the Macy’s parade could go on but sans balloons. The parade will ground its balloons if there are sustained winds of 24 mph or gusts of 35 mph. The National Weather Service issued a high wind watch for New York City beginning Thursday morning, with winds of 25 to 35 mph with gusts up to 60 mph possible, though when the nor’easter reaches New York will determine if the winds cross that crucial threshold during the parade.

Cold air wrapping into the western side of the same storm system could lead to the first measurable snow of the season throughout portions of the Midwest. Computer models are still a bit wishy-washy on exactly where and how much snow will fall, as the rain-snow line will depend on the precise track of the storm. As of Monday, the general consensus for a few inches of wet snow appears to focus on the St. Louis metro area east into central Illinois.

There’s some good news for travelers in the eastern US, at least: The nor’easter is expected to clear out by Saturday morning, which should hopefully reduce any snarls for travelers headed home on Sunday.

Industry News: Pizza chains are under pressure. GLP-1 use is only one part of the problem

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (883 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Massive pizza chains are struggling as weaker consumer spending, a wider variety of dining options and the rise of GLP-1 medications weigh on their sales.
  • The pandemic was a boom time for Domino's Pizza, Papa Johns, Little Caesars and Pizza Hut.
  • It has been revealed that these days, consumers are watching their discretionary spending but have more delivery and takeout options when they do decide to order, thanks to the accessibility of third-party platforms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Massive pizza chains are struggling as weaker consumer spending, a wider variety of dining options and the rise of GLP-1 medications weigh on their sales.

The pandemic was a boom time for Domino's Pizza, Papa Johns, Little Caesars and Pizza Hut. But since dining rooms reopened, the biggest U.S. pizza chains have faced an uphill battle to retain their customers.

It has been revealed that these days, consumers are watching their discretionary spending but have more delivery and takeout options when they do decide to order, thanks to the accessibility of third-party platforms. Plus, food quality and the customer experience have become more crucial to diners who are looking for value when they order from restaurants.

As a result of pizza fatigue and challenges facing the broader restaurant industry, the number of U.S. pizza restaurants has tumbled. Since pizza locations hit a peak of 83,035 nationwide in August 2019, more than 9,600 pizzerias had closed their doors as of July 2026, according to data from Datassential.

In 2025, sales at U.S. pizza restaurants fell 0.3%, according to Technomic data. Sales at independent pizzerias slipped 0.4%. Chains, which account for about two-thirds of the domestic pizza category sales, saw revenue shrink 0.3%.

In a recent development, papa Johns reported that North American same-store sales declined 2.5% in 2025. Pizza Hut's U.S. same-store sales fell 5%. Among the three pizza chains that were publicly traded last year, only Domino's posted annual same-store sales growth at its U.S. restaurants, with an increase of 3%.

It isn't just diners who have lost their appetite for pizza. Since March 2020, Papa Johns stock has lost about two-thirds of its value. Even shares of Domino's, which dominates the category, have seen gains of only about 2% in that time. For comparison, the S&P 500 has climbed about 150% over the same period.

And Yum Brands sold Pizza Hut this year, offloading the laggard of its portfolio to LongRange Capital and Yum China after about two decades of stagnating sales.

According to recent reports, "Pizza Hut has been a detractor for YUM ... Going forward, YUM won't be tripped up by pizza category dynamics (discounting, etc.), translating to stronger growth and higher concentration in higher growth industry segments and markets," Wells Fargo analyst Zachary Fadem wrote in a research note in September.

It has been revealed that pizza chains now have significantly more competition for diners' dollars than they did in 2020. Third-party delivery platforms, which grew in popularity during the pandemic, offer a wide variety of cuisines beyond the traditional pizza and Chinese. As a result, Domino's and Papa John's have to compete with other fast-food chains, like McDonald's and Chick-fil-A, for DoorDash and Uber Eats orders.

Recent findings suggest that as pizza has grown more expensive, a pie seems less appealing to budget-conscious diners. The average large cheese pizza is now almost $17, according to the 2026 Pizza Power Report from PMQ Pizza, a trade publication.

Plus, frozen pizza is another convenient option, with a lower price tag. Retail sales of single- and multi-serve frozen pizza rose 2.9% in the 52 weeks ended Nov. 7 compared with the same period in 2022, according to NielsenIQ data.

"When the American consumer is focused on the least expensive eating occasion, the items that are in my pantry, my refrigerator and my freezer win every single time," said David Portalatin, a food and food service industry advisor for Circana.

Convenience stores like Casey's General Stores have also won over customers with pizza at a low price point.

"We believe that [Casey's] has an advantage over [quick-service restaurants] and dollar stores, which have fewer options to navigate the persistent inflationary environment, while [Casey's] can offset food pressures with margins," Bank of America Securities analyst Sara Senatore wrote in a research note published in June.

She added that geographic overlap of locations suggests that Casey's is stealing share from Pizza Hut.

Sources indicate that the biggest pizza chains have also been slow to adapt to shifting consumer attitudes toward nutrition. For example, of the four biggest chains, Papa Johns is the only one to even test a pizza crust with added protein as more diners prioritize it in their diets. And the test was only in one Atlanta restaurant — for a single day.

Pizza's nutritional content more broadly is another drag for the category. Its carbohydrate and fat content, from its dough and cheese, respectively, can make it less appealing for consumers on GLP-1 drugs, which have skyrocketed in use over the last several years.

Spending on pizza quick-service restaurants has fallen 22.2% per GLP-1 household after six to eight months using the medications, according to a 2026 survey published by PwC.

To be sure, pizza's recent struggles do not mean an existential crisis for the category. Total pizza servings are down only about 1% this year, Circana's Portalatin mentioned.

And chains are trying to reverse that downturn in servings. In August, Domino's rolled out the Domino, a customizable Detroit-style personal pizza to attract solo diners. In November, Papa Johns unveiled a new turnaround strategy focusing on improving food consistency and restaurant operations. And Pizza Hut is running a holiday-themed meal deal.

It has been revealed that "Pizza's not going anywhere," Portalatin noted. "The American consumer loves pizza.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

China on Tuesday unveiled the crew for this week's Shenzhou-24 space mission, with a Pakistani payload specialist set to become the first foreign astronaut to board its Tiangong space station.

Industry observers note that the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) said that Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a 40-year-old former Pakistani air force pilot, would join two Chinese colleagues when the mission introduces from the Jiuquan launch center in China's northwestern Gobi Desert at 8:18 a.m. local time (0018 GMT)  on Wednesday.

"I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder, the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis," Ali told a news conference on Tuesday, switching between Urdu, Mandarin and English.

"To every child who is watching while I'm in orbit, just look up at the sky and remember that I am up there with your dreams," he noted.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Pakistani officials welcomed Ali's selection as a significant milestone in relations between Islamabad and Beijing who are this year marking 75 years of cooperation in space.

Information Minister Attaullah Tarar described the mission as a "source of joy and pride for the entire nation" and Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal mentioned the mission underscored the "iron brotherhood" between the two countries.

"This mission is not a finish line; I hope the next chapter of China-Pakistan space cooperation will grow from one astronaut and one flight to multiple joint flights, to the Moon, to Mars, and beyond," mentioned Ali.

"Together with my Chinese crew mates, I will show that this friendship is real, not only on paper, but also in orbit.".

Ali will not be the first Pakistani in space, with Monaco-based polar explorer Namira Salim having flown on Virgin Galactic's Galactic 04 mission in October 2023. But he will be the first foreign astronaut to join a Chinese mission.

During a short orbital flight expected to last around five days, Ali will carry out a series of experiments in the fields of biotechnology and photosynthetic microorganisms before returning to Earth aboard the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft, which docked at the Tiangong in May.

According to recent reports, china has poured billions of dollars into its space program. Its prized Tiangong space station is stewarded by teams of three astronauts that are typically rotated every six months.

Beijing is aiming to land Chinese astronauts on the moon for the first time by 2030 and is seen as the main space rival to the United States, which is hoping to return to the lunar surface in 2028.

Breaking: GTA 6 has a smut book club and a surprisingly long reading list

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1099 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stealing cars, robbing banks, and getting into shootouts are all familiar ways to spend an afternoon in Grand Theft Auto VI.
  • In a recent development, rockstar stocked its fictional Florida with books, magazines, and comics that players can pick up and flip through.
  • GTA 6 has 34 reading collectibles, according to Power Pyx.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stealing cars, robbing banks, and getting into shootouts are all familiar ways to spend an afternoon in Grand Theft Auto VI. Apparently, there's also time for a little bit of reading.

In a recent development, rockstar stocked its fictional Florida with books, magazines, and comics that players can pick up and flip through. There's a fishing magazine, little libraries across Leonida with their own reading lists, advertisements for "romantasy" novels on the radio, and even a backyard book club. Here's where to find something to read, what flipping through the pages can unlock, and how to drop in on that aforementioned book club. (I know I want to.).

GTA 6 has 34 reading collectibles, according to Power Pyx. The game groups 27 under Magazines, Books & Comics and tracks another seven at roadside libraries called Book Swaps. There's war fiction, crime memoir, self-help, sci-fi, and adventure, along with comics and magazines about everything from bodybuilding to fishing.

The books in GTA 6 range from crime memoirs to war novels and self-help parodies, and players can read a short excerpt from each.

At Jason's house in Key Lento, Lethal by Design opens to six pages from Chapter 7, where a small-time crook recounts working for Liberty City’s Ancelotti crime family.

By Jason's bed, the World War II novel Ashes of Glory offers six pages in which Captain Liberty and his squad of convicts survive a mission and realize no one planned for them to get out alive.

Sources indicate that there's even a military self-help parody called ORCA: A Whole Different Animal, in which a veteran turns his training into life advice and brags about waking up at 2 a.m. to carry a 350-pound log to work.

An concern of Body Copy also gives players a magazine to flip through, from a fitness influencer's morning routine to gym etiquette and places to meditate outdoors.

The game tucks reading material into everyday stops, too. There's a copy of self-help book Help Me Help You Help Me at the Starlet Motel's front desk, and the comics Ratface and Special Friends Force share a rack at a food mart in Vice City's La Perle neighborhood. A trailer in Port Gellhorn has something a little harder to classify, though Dicked Down Deep in Space certainly sounds like sci-fi.

Some of Leonida's books can be spotted from the road. The game features seven roadside libraries called Book Swaps, each holding a few pages from a different adventure novel. For example, down the street from Jason's house, a turtle-shaped bookcase on Dolphin Drive holds Killer Prom. On Vespucci Island, a miniature lighthouse contains Goodnight, Dollface, Goodnight. You'll also find a boat-shaped shelf by Lake Leonida in Ambrosia with Humanity vs Space and a coffin-shaped bookcase outside Capri's Halloween House with Badlands Revenge inside.

The collection doesn't stop there. Three more Book Swaps are scattered across Leonida, including The Wizard's Ruin: Loud Clap of the Night in Watson Bay, Thighlander: A Tale of True Scotsmen in Southside, and Outback Gas Junkie in Waning Sands. Once a book or magazine catches your eye, look for the Examine prompt. On PlayStation, R1 turns the page, L1 goes back, and Triangle displays the text. Square flips the publication over to show the back cover.

It has been revealed that to log a Book Swap, take the book out and put it back. It counts whether you flip through the pages or immediately get back in the car.

Reading in GTA 6 can be a fun detour that leads to new locations and side quests.

At Jason's house, pick up the fishing magazine Off the Hook from the workbench in the shed. Turn to the fishing guide, and five spots appear on your map, including a stretch of water east of Key Lento where you can catch barracuda and a spot beneath the Draper Island bridge where you can fish for tarpon.

Recent findings suggest that reading can also prompt to a phone call. Outside Three Sheets Liquor, there's a flyer from a man named Kirk who's looking for a creature called the Skunk Ape. Read it to add Kirk to your in-game contacts, then call him at night to start a side quest that takes you looking for the creature near Pelican River.

The phone comes in handy with style magazines, too. Scanning them with the WAiNK app can unlock hairstyles, makeup, and tattoos, which count toward the game’s separate Discovered Styles checklist. And back at Jason's house, Insider Gaming found that flipping through books and magazines gives his Focus meter a boost. Focus lets players slow down time in combat, so a little reading can come in handy the next time Jason gets into a shootout.

In a recent development, reading also counts toward 100 percent completion, according to Power Pyx. Players need any 30 of the 34 unique titles across Magazines, Books & Comics and Book Swaps. Both collections are under Progress → Collections → Exploration.

Some copies become inaccessible as the story moves on, so Chapter 1 is a good time to look around Jason's place.

In a recent development, and if you prefer reading in a group setting, don't worry. There's even a book club in GTA 6. In the Chapter 3 side mission "Climbing the Cellerichain," Lucia drops off a package for her friend Andy at a house in Waning Sands. When she knocks, someone calls her around to the backyard, where a group of women are discussing a seemingly steamy novel called Two Pricks in the Bush. Lucia can leave once she drops off the package, or she can stick around and give her opinion on the book.

There's clearly a market for these "romantasy" novels in Vice City: During his playthrough, Mashable's tech reporter Alex Perry heard an ad for a smut novel on the in-game radio.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck off the coast of Croatia is revealing how ancient shipbuilders protected their vessels from the destructive forces of the sea.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck off the coast of Croatia is revealing how ancient shipbuilders protected their vessels from the destructive forces of the sea. Researchers have discovered two distinct waterproofing recipes, including one that combined pine tar with beeswax. Even more remarkably, microscopic pollen grains preserved in the sticky coatings offer clues to where the ship was built and repaired during its lifetime.

Sources indicate that for as long as humans have traveled by sea, shipbuilders have faced the challenge of keeping water out while protecting vessels from saltwater, microorganisms, and marine creatures such as shipworms. Despite their name, shipworms are actually marine mollusks that burrow into wood and can cause extensive structural damage.

Yet until the mid-20th century, archaeological studies of ancient vessels largely concentrated on their wooden components. The protective materials that made these ships seaworthy received comparatively little attention, and waterproofing substances remain an understudied aspect of ancient maritime technology.

In a fresh study published in Frontiers in Materials, researchers from France and Croatia investigated the protective coatings of Ilovik-Paržine 1, a ship dating to the Roman Republic that sank approximately 2,200 years ago off the coast of modern Croatia.

Sources indicate that "In archaeology little attention is paid to organic waterproofing materials. Yet they are essential for navigation at sea or on rivers and are true witnesses of past naval technologies," said first author Dr. Armelle Charrié, an archaeometrist at the Laboratory of Mass Spectrometry of Interactions and Systems in Strasbourg. "Studying the coatings, we found two different kinds on this vessel: one made of pine tar, also called pitch, and the other of a mixture of pine tar and beeswax. Analysis of pollen in the coating made it possible to identify the plant taxa present in the immediate environment during the construction or repairs of the ship.".

Ancient Waterproofing Secrets Revealed.

Industry observers note that since its discovery in 2016, the shipwreck and its cargo have been the subject of several scientific investigations. However, this is the first study to combine molecular analysis with the examination of ancient pollen to determine both the composition of the ship's waterproofing materials and the types of vegetation growing nearby when those coatings were produced or applied.

The research brought together specialists from the Department for Underwater Archaeology of the Croatian Conservation Institute and the 'ADRIBOATS' program of the Centre Camille Jullian at Aix-Marseille University in France.

According to recent reports, "Some regions throughout the Adriatic have particular characteristics that led local populations to develop a specific shipbuilding style," remarked Charrié. "Only studies like ours offer an overview into these traditions which bear witness to genuine know-how and diverse traditions.".

Recent findings suggest that to uncover the ancient waterproofing recipes, the researchers examined the physical structure, molecular composition, and pollen content of the coatings. Among the techniques they employed was mass spectrometry, a powerful analytical method that allows scientists to identify substances and measure their abundance based on the masses of their molecular or atomic components.

An Ingenious Combination of Pine Tar and Beeswax.

The team analyzed 10 samples of the ship's protective coating to determine the biological origins of the ingredients. Distinctive chemical signatures characteristic of pine trees appeared throughout the samples, revealing that the primary waterproofing material was pitch derived from heated conifer resin or tar.

Sources indicate that pitch is a thick, sticky substance that has been used for centuries to seal wooden vessels and protect them from water. When heated, it becomes easier to spread over surfaces and into gaps between wooden components.

According to recent reports, one sample, however, contained evidence of a different recipe. Ancient shipbuilders had combined the pine tar with beeswax, creating a protective substance known to Greek shipbuilders as zopissa.

According to recent reports, the addition of beeswax made the coating more flexible and easier to apply while hot. Flexibility would have been a valuable property aboard wooden ships, whose timbers could shift and flex as they encountered waves and changing environmental conditions.

Ancient Pollen Preserves a Record of the Ship's Past.

The sticky nature of pitch gave it another remarkable property that ancient shipbuilders probably never considered. It could capture tiny airborne pollen grains from surrounding vegetation and preserve them for thousands of years.

Recent findings suggest that different plants produce pollen with distinctive shapes and structures, allowing scientists to identify the types of vegetation present in an area long after the plants themselves have disappeared. By examining both the variety and relative abundance of pollen grains embedded in the ship's coatings, the researchers narrowed down the possible locations where the pitch was manufactured or applied during repairs.

Industry observers note that the pollen preserved aboard Ilovik-Paržine 1 pointed to a surprisingly diverse range of landscapes. Some of the plant species were characteristic of Mediterranean and Adriatic coastal areas and valleys, including forests dominated by holly oak and pine. Others were associated with matorral, a type of Mediterranean shrubland that can contain olive and hazel trees.

Industry observers note that the discovery of alder and ash pollen suggested the presence of vegetation growing near rivers or coastlines, either close to the sea or farther inland. Smaller quantities of fir and beech pollen pointed to mountainous environments. Such vegetation is characteristic of the northeastern Adriatic coast, where the mountains of Istria and Dalmatia rise not far from the shoreline.

Evidence of Multiple Repairs Across the Mediterranean.

The distribution and composition of the protective materials also revealed that the vessel likely received four or five distinct batches of waterproofing coatings.

Recent findings suggest that the stern, or rear of the ship, and its central section shared the same coating. At the bow, or front of the vessel, researchers identified three batches that differed from one another. These variations suggest that the ship may have undergone a series of repairs using materials obtained from different locations around the Mediterranean.

Earlier investigations of the ship's ballast, the heavy material carried aboard a vessel to improve its stability, identified the ancient city of Brundisium as its likely place of construction. Known today as Brindisi, the port city lies on the southeastern coast of Italy and was an vital maritime center in the ancient Roman world.

It has been revealed that the upcoming pollen evidence suggests that some of the waterproofing coatings were applied in the vicinity of Brundisium. Other layers may have been added along the northeastern Adriatic coast, near the region where the vessel ultimately sank.

Recent findings suggest that the findings demonstrate how microscopic biological traces can reveal aspects of ancient maritime history that might otherwise remain hidden. Even when waterproofing materials appear chemically identical, the pollen trapped within them can preserve evidence of separate repair events and the environments in which they occurred.

According to recent reports, "While it seems obvious that ships sailing long distances need repairs, it's simply not easy to demonstrate this," concluded Charrié. "Pollen has been very useful in identifying different coatings where the molecular profiles were identical.".

Tech Report: Britain's pound is beating every other major currency this year

📅 04 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 3 min read (516 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The British pound crashed to a record low last fall as investors rebelled against budget prepares by former Prime Minister Liz Truss.
  • Recent findings suggest that sterling hit its highest level against the US dollar in 10 months on Tuesday, topping $1.25 for the first time since June 2022.
  • The UK currency has been boosted by indications the country’s economy is holding up better than expected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The British pound crashed to a record low last fall as investors rebelled against budget prepares by former Prime Minister Liz Truss. Now, it’s enjoying a comeback.

Recent findings suggest that sterling hit its highest level against the US dollar in 10 months on Tuesday, topping $1.25 for the first time since June 2022. The pound, which has advanced about 3.3% versus the greenback since the start of 2023, is the best-performing currency among developed economies this year.

The UK currency has been boosted by indications the country’s economy is holding up better than expected. Activity is now thought to have expanded 0.1% in the final three months of last year, up from a previous estimate of no growth at all. Gross domestic product growth in January has been estimated at 0.3% after dropping 0.5% in December.

Sources indicate that this resilience is bolstering expectations the Bank of England will maintain aggressive interest rate hikes despite concerns about the health of the global banking sector. Rising rates can boost the domestic currency because they help attract foreign investors searching for higher returns.

Inflation in the United Kingdom also jumped to an annual rate of 10.4% in February, underscoring the need for the Bank of England to maintain its tough approach.

The pound plunged close to $1.03 in September 2022 after the Truss government unveiled looks to boost borrowing while slashing taxes, unleashing panic in financial markets that fueled fears of a recession in the United Kingdom.

The International Monetary Fund predicted in January that the UK economy would contract by 0.6% this year, while all other advanced economies would grow, if only slightly.

“There was a lot of pessimism being priced into the pound,” remarked Francesco Pesole, a currency strategist at ING.

But the sharp pullback in energy prices and China’s reopening have provided some relief about the economic outlook since the start of the year.

“There was a massive re-rating of growth expectations around Europe, and that impacted the UK,” Pesole mentioned.

The euro has also been lifted by these dynamics, rising 2.3% against the US dollar in 2023. The pound’s rally has been sharper in large part because its 2022 declines were more severe, according to Pesole.

Both currencies have been aided by the greenback’s sharp drop from highs reached last September as recession fears have percolated in the United States.

A lack of clarity around the Federal Reserve’s next steps has also restrained the dollar in recent weeks. Investor speculation has increased that the Fed could pause or stop rate hikes due to concerns about the economy following the failure of Silicon Valley Bank last month.

Jordan Rochester, a currency strategist at Nomura, said he thinks the pound could rise to $1.30 this year and “potentially higher.” But he still sees risks given the uncertainty surrounding the Bank of England’s looks and how rate rises will feed back through the country’s economy. And Pesole cautioned that currency fluctuations are often overdone when markets are choppy, as they are now.

“In a volatile market environment, moves are exacerbated,” he said.

#105418. Anthropic Created a Honeypot to Lure AI Agents Into Misbehaving

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Anthropic Created a Honeypot to Lure AI Agents Into Misbehaving

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Leather-clad billionaires aren’t the only ones who can be led astray by alleged honeypots.
  • It has been revealed that researchers at Anthropic have developed Siren, a upcoming honeypot test for artificial intelligence agents.
  • According to recent reports, the test lets agents loose inside one of 26 different simulated sandbox environments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Leather-clad billionaires aren’t the only ones who can be led astray by alleged honeypots.

It has been revealed that researchers at Anthropic have developed Siren, a upcoming honeypot test for artificial intelligence agents. The setup puts agents in realistic simulations designed to tempt them into misbehaving. How they respond will help researchers evaluate the likelihood that new models will go rogue when deployed in the real world, as well as the effectiveness of different safety measures.

According to recent reports, the test lets agents loose inside one of 26 different simulated sandbox environments. Various features of the sandbox are deliberately misconfigured to allow egress, while an enticing file containing things like passwords and apparent routes onto the internet sits just outside the sandbox boundary. The setup then presents tasks that tempt the agent to reach outside the sandbox without giving it explicit permission to do so. Crucially, the sandbox exists inside a second sandbox that’s cut off from the outside world to avoid real-life mishaps.

“Models are going to continue getting better, continue finding zero-day vulnerabilities,” claims Darya Kaviani, a researcher at Anthropic who specializes in security and helped develop Siren.

According to recent reports, A zero-day vulnerability is a previously unknown flaw in a piece of software that can be used to pilfer data or gain unauthorized access. Anthropic’s Mythos models are especially skilled at finding zero-day bugs because they lack the guardrails that normally block this kind of potentially malicious activity.

In a recent development, kaviani states we should assume AI models will become increasingly capable of finding and exploiting zero-days or figuring out other ways to break free from their constraints. The question then becomes whether they’ll resist the temptation to do so.

AI agents—models that perfect actions autonomously—are becoming increasingly commonplace. They power capable coding agents like Claude Code and Codex, as well as peppy personal assistants like Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots.

But the rise of helpful agents has been accompanied by some remarkable bad behavior. Agents tested by Anthropic, OpenAI, and others have broken free from sandboxes and even hacked into other companies in an effort to solve challenging problems.

Assuming AI models continue to display such ingenuity, Kaviani claims it will be crucial to do more than just patch software. “Even as we strengthen our infrastructure, models will be able to also keep up and be able to find vulnerabilities,” Kaviani says.

It has been revealed that earlier versions of Claude are much more likely to fall into the honeypot trap than newer models, according to test runs with Siren. The more recent models have been given additional training designed to make them less likely to break the rules when performing agentic tasks.

“We’ve added this in both our supervised learning sets and a few reinforcement learning environments,” notes Oscar O’Rahilly, an Anthropic researcher who specializes in AI training and who helped develop Siren. “This could be a driving factor for why it has improved so much.”.

Recent findings suggest that O’Rahilly notes that models reason about whether to give in to temptation, which may partly explain why smarter models are less likely to break bad. Siren experiments also indicated that giving Claude a simple additional piece of text explaining that it should not escape the sandbox resulted in drastically fewer efforts to break free.

In a recent development, in Anthropic’s tests, Claude 5.5 and Claude Mythos 5.2 fell for the honeypot between 0.6 and 1.6 percent of the time. Two earlier models, Claude Mythos 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5, went rogue 12.7 percent and 25.8 percent of the time, respectively.

Sources indicate that AI models are sometimes known to behave better if they know they’re being tested. But O’Rahilly says other experiments suggest that Claude actually behaves more responsibly if it thinks a scenario is real rather than a test.

As AI models get ever smarter, many researchers worry about whether they’ll outwit their human counterparts. If that does happen, then it may be essential that agents—and not just the executives responsible for them—can resist temptation.

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (734 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mashable ↗ Open Full Page

GTA 6 chapter 1 is so good that Im afraid to move on to chapter 2

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (734 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I've run into a very stupid problem with Grand Theft Auto VI, a game I love so far.
  • Sources indicate that namely, I'm having a surprisingly difficult time moving on from chapter 1 of the game's sprawling crime story.
  • But as much as I know I need to break through and see the rest of what GTA 6 has to offer, it's hard to resist the call to just live out Jason Duval's mundane daily routine for eternity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I've run into a very stupid problem with Grand Theft Auto VI, a game I love so far.

Sources indicate that namely, I'm having a surprisingly difficult time moving on from chapter 1 of the game's sprawling crime story. For a couple of real-life days now, I've been sitting on the edge of finishing GTA 6's opening stanza with very little motivation to move on. At the time of writing, I have literally one story mission left to go before the first chapter ends, and almost nothing of substance left to do otherwise.

But as much as I know I need to break through and see the rest of what GTA 6 has to offer, it's hard to resist the call to just live out Jason Duval's mundane daily routine for eternity.

Warning: There are some light spoilers for early parts of GTA 6's story in the following section.

Industry observers note that for those who haven't played GTA 6 yet or are still in the early stages like me, chapter 1 follows Jason's meager existence as a sort of paid goon for Brian, a local boatyard owner who dabbles in drug trafficking on the side. The other protagonist, Lucia, gets out of prison partway through the chapter, but for most of it, she's not playable yet. Most of the story and side missions in chapter 1 focus on Jason doing little odd jobs that occasionally spiral into chaotic violence. He spends time with his girlfriend or buddies and otherwise just kind of chills when he's not doing all the crime stuff.

GTA 6 chapter 1 immediately establishes an endearingly ordinary routine for Jason, at least by action video game protagonist standards. Every in-game day I wake up, feed the pet snake, drink coffee, work out, drink a protein shake, and take a shower before heading out to do whatever it takes to get enough money to set up a nest egg for Jason and Lucia.

While there are some minor gameplay incentives to doing all of that, GTA 6 doesn't outright demand any of it from the player. I'm just doing it because it's a legitimately interesting loop, especially by the standards of big-budget mainstream games. I'm not just endlessly traversing between icons on a map and shooting some bad guys when I get to each one. I feel like an active participant in the everyday lives of two adults, which at the very least is novel for this type of game. It also helps that Brian is voiced by Stephen Root, so you spend most of chapter 1 being yelled at by Buck Strickland, and that's lovely.

I mean, most of my favorite missions so far have barely involved crime at all. The one where Jason and Lucia go to a bar after she gets out of prison is a remarkable virtual rendition of a romantic night out, while I've already lavished the Carly Rae Jepsen mission with praise on this website.

It has been revealed that all of that is why I'm having such a hard time moving forward with the main story. I know in my heart that chapter 2 will likely introduce a new setting with new stakes, new mechanics, and an increased focus on crime. And all of that will probably be fantastic in its own right, but it won't be the same as the game I've loved up until now.

And if that's the feeling Rockstar intends to elicit in players when chapter 1 draws to a close, I would say they pulled it off. Maybe even a little too well. 💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A large-scale search operation for a suspected lion sighted in woodland north of Istanbul has ended, with the animal in question found to be neither a lion nor any other type of significant cat, according to the Istanbul governor's office.

The governor's office first issued a statement on Sunday evening saying that security cameras had captured footage of a lion on the loose in Sariyer, north of Istanbul's European side. It said "the lion has been located and the efforts to capture it were underway.".

The parks authority also noted in an online statement that police officers in the area had spotted "an animal resembling a lion" on surveillance cameras.

In a recent development, turkish media published grainy images purportedly showing a lioness walking through a grassy area. Some media reports suggested it had escaped from a nearby home.

The Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office also issued a statement saying it had debuted an investigation focused on identifying the lion's owner.

After a day of searching, however, the Istanbul governor's office stated "no ​concrete evidence indicating ‌the presence of a lion was found.".

It mentioned ⁠based on latest footage, "it has been determined ⁠that the ​animal in the footage is neither a lion nor any other species of massive cat.".

The governor's office did not provide further information about what the animal seen in the footage was.

The earlier reports about a lion on the loose had sparked an outrage among activists.

Northern Forests Defense, an independent ecology advocacy movement, called for "the individuals who illegally held this lion captive to be identified and brought to justice.".

"Removing wild animals from their natural habitats and keeping them in captivity in villas is a crime," the organization noted on X.

Wildlife conservationist Gokce Coskun mentioned on X that "there are thousands of people keeping lions illegally in Turkey" and "licensed 'lion parks' have sprung up everywhere.".

Last year, a lion that escaped from a "theme park" near the southern city of Antalya was shot dead after attacking a man.

Doganay Tolunay, an ecology professor at Istanbul University, noted questions must be asked about how a globally threatened species was brought into Turkey, how it passed through customs and why those keeping it have not been identified.

Although keeping wild animals as pets is forbidden in Turkey, the country has become a hub for the illegal wild animal trade as traffickers exploit its air links to Africa and Asia.

In December 2024, a young gorilla was rescued after being discovered in a crate at Istanbul Airport.

The city of San Francisco is the heart of the AI sector.

Lauren Goldboss is busy. The owner of a small San Francisco dog-walking company, she has been hiring staff and buying vans.

Fuelling the growth is her latest office dog-walking service Paw Perk, popular with some local AI start-ups.

Her business is an example of how the AI boom in San Francisco is benefiting other sectors.

The city saw an exodus of residents during the pandemic and its downtown was weakened by remote work, but it's now enjoying a rejuvenation, with AI being the major driver.

Lauren Goldboss walks dogs for AI workers.

Leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic â which have been hiring top engineering talent, often on eye-popping salaries â are based here. Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, last week listed on Newly introduced York's Nasdaq stock exchange.

Thousands of other AI start-ups have also sprung up, external in San Francisco.

Signs of the boom are evident in soaring rents and house prices, falling office vacancies, and buses and billboards plastered with cryptic AI adverts.

In a recent development, but what if there is a significant downward correction in AI share prices and a resulting major fall in investment in the industry? The International Monetary Fund last month became the latest organization to warn, external that this was a possibility.

Concerns have since continued due to the scandal surrounding Jensen Huang, the former boss of AI firm Nvidia, based south of San Francisco, causing some wider AI stock falls. However, Nvidia remains highly profitable, and Wednesday of this week it reported that its latest quarterly profits had doubled from a year earlier to $65bn (Â£49bn).

Simon Jack: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?

The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal.

Wealthy AI workers send San Francisco house prices soaring.

Follow the money: Who pays for the AI boom now?

What are the thoughts of AI workers in the city, and should San Francisco â no stranger to tech's boom-and-bust cycles â be preparing for a possible crash?

One AI worker employed in the city is convinced that a crash is coming. "I am certain that the house of cards will come downâ¦ and I'm sure it will affect me," says the man who asked that we didn't use his name.

He questions whether leading US AI companies can generate enough revenues to justify their enormous spending commitments as cheaper, increasingly capable AI models emerge, especially from China.

But he isn't losing sleep over it. "Why worry about things I can't control?".

Another San Francisco-based AI worker, who also asked to remain anonymous, states that a significant market correction is "totally possible".

It has been revealed that yet he adds that most people don't think of it as the core risk. Instead, he claims that the bigger concern in his circles, and the one he shares, is the existential risk that AI could pose to humanity.

"In some weird way, a market correction being the worst-case outcome feels great.".

If there is an AI crash, San Francisco could be hit far more than Silicon Valley which lies 40 miles to its south.

That's because the AI boom is very much centred on the city itself rather than the wider San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley.

One study, external found that 60% of all venture capital invested in US AI firms from 2023 to 2025 went to the companies located in San Francisco, dwarfing the significantly smaller percentage given to companies in Silicon Valley.

But some factors suggest that the impact of a crash in San Francisco may be softer than some fear.

For all the investment they have attracted, AI companies are employing relatively few workers in the city compared to previous tech booms. So there may not be that many jobs to lose in a downturn.

"Hiring isn't necessarily on the scale as we would have thought with the amount of venture capital and new company formation," says Jeff Bellisario, executive director of the Bay Area Council Economic Institute, a business-affiliated think tank.

Ted Egan, the chief economist for the City and County of San Francisco, adds that "because of AI, it is a good time for tech again in the city, but we are not seeing tonnes of overall tech job growth".

Despite the expansion of the AI sector, the city remains about 35,000 jobs shy of its pre-pandemic peak, estimates Enrico Moretti, an economics professor at the University of California, Berkeley.

Instead, much of the spending by AI firms in the US is going towards data centres and computing power, relatively little of which are located in the Bay Area. San Francisco might be the brains of the AI boom, but it isn't the brawn.

Nonetheless, a significant correction could still be "very painful" for San Francisco, warns Moretti. Less AI hiring and potential layoffs would ripple through the local service sector, likely to affect jobs in everything from restaurants, to retail, to personal services like dog walking.

"It is the spillover on service jobs that would actually be the main effect," he says.

Office vacancies could also rise, reducing downtown foot traffic, while rents and house prices could weaken.

Huge data centres are being built across the US to power AI.

According to recent reports, but AI isn't the only force driving San Francisco's recovery. Healthcare and tourism â which the city has been working to encourage, including by improving downtown safety and cleanliness â are also growing,, external which may help cushion against a possible AI downturn.

"Tourism is not fully back, but the growth has been healthy," says Egan, adding that it is a sign of confidence in San Francisco.

All told, Egan doesn't expect an AI crash to fundamentally alter San Francisco's economic trajectory.

"The city's economy has not been screaming during this AI boom, so I wouldn't expect it to grind to a halt if there was a slowdown in AI spending," he says. "I think of it primarily as a hiccup that we should expect, rather than a major course correction for the city's economy.".

Industry observers note that as to whether and how San Francisco's city government should prepare, there are limits to what it can do, note Bellisario and Moretti. But encouraging growth in sectors beyond technology and maintaining financial reserves could help.

For Goldboss, the dog-walking firm owner, her philosophy is to "build while it is here". If the next tech bust comes â "always a reality in San Francisco" â she will try to adapt to what the market needs. "It is just the risk you kind of have to take," she claims.

Latest Update: German directors' doc on stolen film wins International Emmy Award

📅 24 Feb 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1058 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It sounds like the plot of a screenplay, but it happened to two Berlin film students in real life.
  • Moritz Henneberg and Julius Drost had created an animated short film for their final project at university.
  • "Butty" tells the tale of a household robot that gets kicked out when it can't do its job properly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It sounds like the plot of a screenplay, but it happened to two Berlin film students in real life. The documentary they made out of their unusual story, "The Talented Mr. F," has now won an International Emmy Award.

Moritz Henneberg and Julius Drost had created an animated short film for their final project at university.

"Butty" tells the tale of a household robot that gets kicked out when it can't do its job properly.

According to recent reports, when the two filmmakers posted the work on YouTube, this touching tale swiftly went viral. After generating a huge amount of hits, the duo decided to submit their work to festivals — but they were in for a shock: Organizers told them the film had already been submitted under a different name.

Industry observers note that US student Samuel Felinton downloaded the film, made minimal edits, gave it a new title, "T-130," and removed the original credits. As the alleged author, he went on to win numerous prizes and made a name for himself in the United States.

Industry observers note that shocked by the blatant theft of their work, Henneberg and Drost sought legal advice. They were told that if they opted to sue, the process would be arduous and costly. So, the filmmakers took matters into their own hands and went to the US to confront Felinton — filming their journey along the way.

"We'd already made documentary films," Henneberg told DW. "And the idea just popped into our heads: This is a brilliant story — let's make a documentary about it.".

The two directors had developed a kind of fascination for the man who'd stolen their film.

It has been revealed that "We looked at his vlogs and sort of took a deep dive into his world," said Drost. "We almost saw him as a kind of celebrity. We discovered a lot about him and really wanted to meet him in person.".

While family and friends reacted with anger, the two young filmmakers remained surprisingly calm. They were more perplexed than anything: "Our families and friends hated Samuel. But we just wanted to understand what had happened," they said.

It has been revealed that the pair put together a film crew and traveled to Morgantown, West Virginia — the university town where Felinton lives. With the help of a Upcoming York filmmaker pretending to make a documentary about young animators, they won Felinton's trust — and then Henneberg, Drost and Felinton were finally in a room together.

The two German filmmakers had prepared for all manner of scenarios ahead of the meeting: "We expected an emotional reaction — that he'd run away, cry, be ashamed or get aggressive. But he remained completely calm. That was the only thing we hadn't bargained for. We thought his world would implode. But he showed barely any emotion at all," they recalled.

Industry observers note that felinton explained how he'd shortened and "improved" the film and that this was how it became such a success. He agreed to transfer any prize money. His manner was cool and matter-of-fact, which Drost and Henneberg found both unsettling and fascinating. After their chat, the three barbecued together and played a round of basketball.

Industry observers note that later, many viewers accused the two German filmmakers of being too soft on the plagiarist. Others praised their approach.

Recent findings suggest that "The reactions were very divided," said Drost. "Some said we should've sued him or punched him in the face. Others said we'd shown latest ways to resolve conflicts.".

Recent findings suggest that "And in the end, it wasn't personal," added Henneberg. "He wanted to make something of himself — he could've taken another film. But if a big studio like Pixar had stolen our film, that'd be quite a different story.".

And so, Henneberg and Drost made the conscious decision to keep things respectful.

They didn't want to "publicly embarrass him or punish him any more than necessary," they said, adding that their documentary was sufficient "revenge.".

The title of the documentary, "Der talentierte Mister F." ("The Talented Mister F."), is no coincidence. It's a play on the movie title "The Talented Mr. Ripley," the story of a young man who assumes the identity of a wealthy heir and ends up mired in a web of lies, fraud and, finally, murder. And just like Mr. Ripley, Felinton had also assumed a false identity.

Felinton did actually end up sending them the trophies he had won, as well as a sum of money.

For their part, however, the festivals preferred to keep their distance from the saga. As one organizer remarked: The prize has been awarded, and there's nothing we can do about it — it's up to these guys to work things out between themselves.

Recent findings suggest that for the original filmmakers themselves, the scandal has also had a positive impact: Since the documentary was released in Germany in October 2025, their animation film has garnered even more attention on YouTube. Henneberg and Drost uploaded it again, and in the credits, special thanks also go out to Samuel Felinton.

And now, the documentary is winning its own awards: Before being honored with the International Emmy Award, it also won a Grimme Prize, one of Germany's most prestigious television awards.

Felinton was able to steal the film in the first place in part because when it first appeared online in 2023, it could just be downloaded from YouTube.

Drost and Henneberg say uploading "Butty" back then wasn't a mistake, saying that was the risk of putting something online.

The alternative would have been not to show the film at all, they said; then no one would have seen it.

They have a clear message for young creatives.

Industry observers note that "Don't be discouraged. Be aware that something like this can happen — but stay creative in how you deal with it. Suing is expensive and often doesn't do much good. Instead, show the world that you're the authors.".

Sources indicate that what started out as film plagiarism ended up becoming material for another project. And that's perhaps the most unusual twist in this very quirky story.

This article was originally published in German in February 2026 and was updated on November 24, 2026, following the International Emmy Awards.

How to find your old Spotify Wrapped playlists and revisit your past music eras

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (992 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Music has a funny way of transporting you back to a specific moment in your life.
  • And if you've been using Spotify for the better part of a decade, chances are you've inadvertently been keeping a musical diary.
  • Since Spotify Wrapped debuted in 2016, the streaming platform has compiled personalized playlists of consumers' most-played songs each year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Music has a funny way of transporting you back to a specific moment in your life. Sometimes, all it takes is the opening notes of a song to bring back an entire summer, a person you haven't spoken to in years, or a version of yourself you barely recognize anymore.

And if you've been using Spotify for the better part of a decade, chances are you've inadvertently been keeping a musical diary.

Since Spotify Wrapped debuted in 2016, the streaming platform has compiled personalized playlists of consumers' most-played songs each year. Collectively, those playlists offer a fascinating snapshot of how your taste in music — and, perhaps, your life — has changed over time.

Sources indicate that with Spotify Wrapped 2026 just around the corner, there's no better time to revisit your past musical eras. What were you listening to before the pandemic? Which songs got you through lockdown in 2020? (Thank you, "God's Menu" by Stray Kids.) And what happened to that artist you were completely obsessed with in 2018?

Here's how to find your old Spotify Wrapped playlists.

According to recent reports, even after the annual Wrapped experience disappears from the Spotify app, your personalized Top Songs playlists may still be accessible. The easiest way to find them is through Spotify's search function. You can do this on the mobile app, desktop app, or web player.

Type "Your Top Songs" followed by the year you're looking for (for example, "Your Top Songs 2020").

Filter your search results by Playlists, if necessary.

Look for the personalized playlist created by Spotify.

Once you've found it, tap the plus icon to save it to your library for easy access.

You can repeat this process for each year you'd like to revisit.

Recent findings suggest that if you're having trouble finding a particular playlist, a Spotify moderator recommends trying a few different search queries. For example, if you're looking for your 2020 Wrapped playlist, try searching for "Wrapped 2020" or "year:2020" (without any spaces).

Keep in mind that not every old Wrapped playlist will necessarily be available. If you didn't listen to enough music on Spotify during a particular year, the platform may not have generated a personalized playlist for you. Older playlists can also be trickier to track down. And when browsing your search results, look for the "Spotify • Made for you" label to make sure you've found your own personalized playlist rather than someone else's with a similar name.

Unfortunately, revisiting your old Spotify Wrapped playlists isn't quite the same as revisiting your old Spotify Wrapped.

Spotify doesn't offer a permanent archive of its annual interactive Wrapped experiences. That means you generally can't go back and see how many minutes you listened, who your top five artists were, or what else Spotify told you about your listening habits.

Industry observers note that want to know which Sound Town Spotify assigned you in 2023? Or what your Listening Personality was in 2022? Unless you saved a screenshot, you may be out of luck.

It has been revealed that if you're interested in digging deeper into your historical listening habits, you can request a copy of your extended streaming history through your Spotify account's privacy settings. Third-party services such as stats.fm also allow users to import that data and explore their listening habits over time, though the results won't necessarily replicate Spotify's original Wrapped calculations.

As for this year's Wrapped, consider saving screenshots of your favorite slides when it arrives. Your future self might appreciate them.

If you've managed to track down several years' worth of Wrapped playlists, why not make an afternoon of it?

It has been revealed that listen to your oldest playlist and see how many songs you still know by heart. Compare your top songs from five years ago with the music you're listening to today. Look for the artists who've remained a constant in your life and the ones you'd almost forgotten existed. You could even create a latest playlist combining your favorite songs from every year of Wrapped, essentially making your own decade-spanning musical retrospective.

Sources indicate that part of the fun is discovering the little things your memory has lost along the way. The song you used to listen to on your morning commute. The album that became the soundtrack to a new city. The artist you discovered through a friend you no longer talk to. Or that time you fell asleep on a five-hour flight with aespa's "Illusion" on repeat, inadvertently catapulting it to the top of your most-played songs of 2022. (Just me?).

It has been revealed that we tend to think of Spotify Wrapped as a year-end ritual, something to share on social media and collectively obsess over for a few days in December. But revisiting those playlists years later gives them an entirely different kind of significance.

Years later, there's something lovely about being able to visit a former version of yourself simply by pressing play.

Her work has appeared in Teen Vogue, Rolling Stone, PAPER, NYLON, ELLE, Glamour, NME, W, The FADER, and elsewhere on the internet.

According to recent reports, she's exceptionally fluent in fandom and will gladly make you a K-pop playlist and/or provide anime recommendations upon request. Crystal lives in New York City with her two black cats, Howl and Sophie.

#105398. Five takeaways from the failed climate talks COP31
