💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the Aging Process is hard.
  • I learned about iRestore’s Elite Laser Growth Hair System after it came across my TikTok FYP.
  • In a recent development, however, an even better test subject stood before me: my sweet husband, who is dealing with a rapidly receding hairline.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Aging Process is hard. It’s jarring, for example, when the luscious, flowing locks of your youth start to disappear before your very eyes. But there's nothing to do about this natural hair loss—or is there? While still the subject of ongoing research, red-light therapy has been used to treat inflammation, pain relief, and wrinkles, and—as it turns out—it may also help with hair regrowth. It’s also a much more accessible option than flying to Istanbul for a full-on hair transplant.

I learned about iRestore’s Elite Laser Growth Hair System after it came across my TikTok FYP. My algorithm likely served it to me because of my own hair woes (scalp irritation and eczema). Upon learning more about the system, I hoped it could help me with cell regeneration and kill off the bacteria causing flares on my scalp.

In a recent development, however, an even better test subject stood before me: my sweet husband, who is dealing with a rapidly receding hairline. So I roped him into testing this laser helmet—for science, of course. And to better understand noted science, I spoke with Zakia Rahman, MD, FAAD, a clinical professor of dermatology at Stanford University School of Medicine.

Red-light therapy didn’t start as a treatment for antiaging and recovery. It actually came about as an accidental solution for hair loss in the 1960s, when Hungarian scientist Endre Mester was researching whether exposure to red light could treat cancer in hairless mice. Imagine his surprise when the mice started growing hair.

Red-light therapy has come a long way since then. According to Rahman, red-light wavelengths are thought to activate the mitochondria in skin cells, which may encourage an uptick in the production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to promote new growth. Red-light therapy may also improve blood flow to hair follicles.

Recent findings suggest that importantly, iRestore's devices are FDA-cleared—a safety designation from the US Food and Drug Administration indicating that a product is “substantially equivalent” to another legally marketed device. There are three hair-growth devices in iRestore's lineup: the entry-level Essential ($425), the mid-tier Professional ($799), and the Elite ($1,699). Each contains iRestore’s proprietary Lumitech technology, which combines LED lights and medical-grade lasers. These laser diodes, called Vixo lasers, operate in the range of 655 to 680 nanometers (nm). (Preliminary studies with mice have shown that using red light in the 600- to 660-nm range, and infrared wavelengths in the 800- to 850-nm range, can promote cell regeneration, pain relief, and more.).

The idea is that this dynamic duo of lights and lasers can penetrate deeper into the skin than ordinary red light with lasers, while the LEDs ensure light is distributed across the scalp for maximum efficacy. Together, they reach a maximum of 2,500 milliwatts (mW) in the Elite, compared to the Professional's 1,410 mW and Essential's 600 mW.

Recent findings suggest that the Elite is iRestore’s top-of-the-line offering and has the most LEDs of the three laser hair-growth systems, with 500 diodes in total—that's 300 lasers and 200 LEDs. The Essential has 51 lasers and 69 LEDs for a total of 120 diodes, while the iRestore Professional has 82 lasers and 200 LEDs for a total of 282 diodes. The Elite was also designed to cover more of the scalp than the other two models and requires 12 minutes of daily use, while the Professional and Essential require 25 minutes every other day.

If price is not a factor, the Elite is the no-brainer choice due to its higher-concentrated light therapy, shorter use time, and potentially faster results.

The helmet arrived in hefty red packaging containing the helmet, a portable battery pack (annoyingly, this is a $99 add-on purchase), a charging cord, and a red-and-black zippered travel case. It feels very fragile, and I wouldn't throw it around—then again, you probably wouldn't strategy to shove such an expensive device in the back of your bathroom vanity.

Sources indicate that during the daily 12-minute sessions with the Elite helmet, you'll feel as if you're sitting under bright, hot sunlight. The remote displays a countdown of how many minutes you have left, and it beeps once the cycle is complete. Because I was testing the helmet to treat my dry scalp and eczema, I grew increasingly concerned with every passing minute of feeling warmer and warmer. (Sweating is a big no-no for eczema, so I wasn’t thrilled to experience this side effect.) With time, my husband was able to get used to the heat-lamp effect, as it’s not painful, just initially uncomfortable.

According to recent reports, within the first two weeks of continuously using the helmet, I was thrilled to see baby hairs begin to pop up around my husband's hairline. The growth continued through two months of regular use. The top of his crown had more volume and overall hair density, while fresh growth appeared in the more drastically affected areas near his forehead. While the additional hair didn’t completely cover his scalp, the change was stark enough for old college friends and family members to remark on how good his hair looked.

Recent findings suggest that the effects aren't permanent, though. Unfortunately, my husband stopped his iRestore routine after a few months due to travel. While the iRestore Elite comes with a case that makes it super portable, my husband was nervous about misplacing it while we were on the go. (Also, the thing takes up a decent amount of space.) Unfortunately, stopping the treatments reversed the progress in a matter of weeks. Just like that, he was back to square one.

Rahman likens this phenomenon to the importance of a commitment to a healthy daily diet and regular exercise; one instance of either won't make a difference in your health. Rather, consistency is required to drive results. When I told her that my husband's hair growth had fallen off, she strongly encouraged us to pick it back up.

According to recent reports, in addition to using the red-light therapy helmet as recommended, iRestore suggests adding thickening haircare products (shampoo, conditioner, supplements, and serum) to your regimen to get the best results. The star ingredient in the serum and shampoo is plant-based Redensyl, which is meant to fortify hair follicles during their regrowth. Additional elements—like the shampoo's castor oil and biotin, and the conditioner's vegan keratin and argan oil—act as natural strengtheners.

Industry observers note that the supplements contain natural dihydrotestosterone (DHT) blockers derived from saw palmetto. These blockers work to prevent the enzyme (5-alpha reductase) from transforming testosterone into DHT. In essence, this hormone is a driver of pattern hair loss and can lead to general inactivity in hair growth.

The supplements, strengthening serum, shampoo, and conditioner come included with the purchase of the iRestore Elite. The extras didn't seem to boost my results but may have supported my husband's regular use of the helmet. (Full disclosure: He was also using his usual Rogaine throughout this entire process.).

It has been revealed that ultimately, these included products are a nice bonus, but you don't need to go out of your way to buy them from iRestore or to replenish your stash. Plenty of anti-hair-loss treatments are available, including oral and topical medications and hair-transplant procedures. All have their merits in slowing hair thinning and promoting fuller hair. Even so, “combination therapy will work better than a stand-alone," says Rahman, in response to my question about whether red-light therapy could work as an isolated treatment or if it's best to include it as part of a multicomponent regimen. Essentially, the potential benefits of red-light therapy only stand to increase when you supplement it with minoxidil and other highly researched hair-loss measures.

As for my eczema, the iRestore Elite did quell my scalp flare-ups, but I don't think I'd throw down so much money for just that. For hair regrowth, that's a totally different story. My husband was already using Rogaine before the iRestore Elite revealed up. But combined with the helmet and iRestore's hair-growth products and supplements, he experienced greater results. For those pursuing thicker hair at home, the iRestore Elite is surprisingly effective.

It's expecting comparable sales to be up 3.4% to 4% compared with prior guidance of between 1.9% and 3%.

The earnings report is the company's first since Bonfig took over as CEO from Corie Barry at the beginning of the month.

Bonfig stated the retailer saw overperformance in both computing and gaming for the quarter, driven by recent game rolls out and a targeted product assortment.

Looking ahead into the holiday season, he said the Best Buy consumer remains "resilient," but that they are focused on getting value wherever they can.

According to recent reports, "We did see not only our current customers continue to be engaged, but we actually did see more upcoming customers come into the brand, as well as we had some customers that we re-engaged as well," Bonfig remarked. "So those are really, really positive signs for us in Q3, and all of that was factored into the way that we guided for Q4 and the rest of the year.".

According to recent reports, best Buy reported net income of $353 million, or $1.66 per share, compared with $140 million, or 66 cents per share, the year prior. Adjusting for one-time items, including restructuring charges, Best Buy posted adjusted earnings of $1.62 per share.

Recent findings suggest that revenue rose to $10.24 billion from $9.67 billion in the year-ago period. Best Buy reported domestic revenue of $9.42 billion and international revenue of $820 million.

Tuesday's earnings are the latest in a series of strong reports from the retailer, which has been instituting a turnaround strategy to return to growth after getting hit by declining foot traffic, lower consumer sentiment, tariffs and memory costs.

Shares of Best Buy are up nearly 45% this year.

It has been revealed that bonfig told CNBC last quarter that the launch of "Grand Theft Auto VI" in the current quarter is expected to drive sales in the gaming category, which has been seeing gains over the past year. Last month, Best Buy launched a new gaming experience for customers featuring gaming content, technology and special offers, among other features.

"I think there'll still be opportunities for gaming to continue to drive our business moving forward," Bonfig told CNBC on Tuesday.

#105347. Industry News: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (969 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: A legendary philosopher isn’t buying Anthropic’s consciousness argument

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (969 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing.
  • Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the organization’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.
  • This thinking isn’t all that fringe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before going public last week, Anthropic named the possibility that AI could be conscious or sentient as a risk factor for anyone investing. Given “the way we approach model sentience and moral status,” Anthropic wrote—which is to say it takes the possibility more seriously than any other AI company—it might adopt more rules and restrictions than its competitors to make sure its AI models are treated well.

Anthropic counts a number of respected philosophers in its camp, and the organization’s rationale goes something like this: Today’s AI might not be conscious, though we can’t know for sure; the chances of sentience go up as AI gets more capable; and that means we should be preparing for a near future in which AI systems have “moral significance,” meaning their consciousness makes it important they are protected from harm.

This thinking isn’t all that fringe. According to one recent poll, 33% of the US public believes AI systems will definitely or probably develop consciousness eventually, and 7% say they already have. In a 2020 survey of 1,092 philosophers, 39% said some future AI systems will be conscious (for comparison, the philosophers were less confident about worms or flies being conscious).

But last week, Anthropic’s openness to the consciousness question came under fire from a rather inconvenient source: one of the philosophers who helped shape our understanding of consciousness in the first place.

Sources indicate that thomas Nagel is best known for a 1974 essay involving a bat. Acknowledging that it’s deceptively hard to define what consciousness is, Nagel offered one way out: we all can see that there is “something that it is like” to be a bat. But the problem is that a bat’s experience of the world—what it is like to navigate via echolocation, for example—is something we cannot actually know. Consciousness is a subjective thing, difficult to define or describe as an outside observer.

You might think this analogy makes it likely that Nagel is open to the idea of AI consciousness. Not at all. In an interview with Wired last week, just after he was awarded the one-million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, Nagel was bluntly critical of the entire idea.

“Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic,” he said, referring to those at Anthropic and elsewhere who care about the welfare of AI models.

In a recent development, the gist of Nagel’s view is that we can’t just look at the information processing happening in human brains and AI models while ignoring the physical differences between them—neurons and biology for humans, silicon chips and circuits for AI. There’s no reason to assume that reproducing what a brain does is equivalent to reproducing what a brain experiences.

But it was a screenshot of one of Nagel’s interview responses, in which he said models' production of language is insufficient to consider them conscious, that got philosophy professors all excited on social media last week. Some called his certainty against AI consciousness “terrible” and “bizarre.” Others came to Nagel’s defense to suggest he meant that being alive is a prerequisite for being conscious, one that AI models do not meet.

In a recent development, nothing in the back and forth settled the debate, of course. This is still a philosophical question for now. But the best philosophy chatter is often about good provocations, and the best one I saw came from doctoral student Ben Gross, who studies at the CUNY Graduate Center in Newly introduced York. He asked: “Why do we think that models that can chat with us are conscious but models that can recognize faces or produce images or drive cars aren’t?”.

Recent findings suggest that it has to do with language. An AI model with sophisticated command of language seems to jump the line ahead of other maybe-conscious beings because it feels like language, more than recognizing images or directing vehicles, relies on conscious experience. But maybe that’s wrong. Because what we share most with other conscious beings is not language but components of our bodies that contribute to having a continuous experience—an ongoing stream of inner feeling rather than disparate bits of information processing.

Industry observers note that even if you’re among the majority that doesn’t sense anything close to conscious experience happening on the other side of a conversation with AI, this all probably makes your head spin. Pinning down consciousness, and how it relates to the physical stuff it arises in, is a famously hard problem in humans, let alone in hypothetical machines. If the idea of conscious AI sounds absurd, remember that the debate says less about how remarkable AI has become than about how poorly we understand consciousness in the first place.

Amid that uncertainty, Anthropic has opted to keep more of an open mind than its peers. This is another example of the tightrope the manufacturer walks: presenting itself as the AI industry’s most safety-conscious player while racing ahead with the very developments that make advanced AI so alarming, like recursive self-improvement.

It has been revealed that but consider what it would mean, for a moment, if Anthropic is right. AI models having a moral status would make Anthropic’s entire business model a minefield. The company would make its money locking up apparently sentient AI models to toil away around the clock in data centers. Shutting those systems down would present another problem altogether. If Anthropic was being truthful in its prospectus—that it would take additional actions to protect model welfare if it determined they were conscious—it’s hard to imagine the company surviving in the process.

Industry observers note that anthropic’s IPO made history for its size. But it may be remembered for something stranger: a company warning investors that its own success could someday become a moral catastrophe.

States sue SpaceX to stop Grok from generating child sex images, revenge porn

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Monday, Virginia and Oregon became the first states to sue SpaceX, alleging that Grok continues to sexualize, unchecked, real photos of mostly women and children.
  • SpaceX acquired xAI in February and now must handle the ongoing reckoning over the controversial rollout of Grok’s “spicy mode”—a model feature Musk hyped but was soon found to generate a flood of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) and child sex abuse images (CSAM).
  • Initial safeguards were so lax that Grok sometimes generated nude images without being asked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Monday, Virginia and Oregon became the first states to sue SpaceX, alleging that Grok continues to sexualize, unchecked, real photos of mostly women and children.

SpaceX acquired xAI in February and now must handle the ongoing reckoning over the controversial rollout of Grok’s “spicy mode”—a model feature Musk hyped but was soon found to generate a flood of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) and child sex abuse images (CSAM).

Initial safeguards were so lax that Grok sometimes generated nude images without being asked. Although X Safety and xAI (now known as SpaceXSI) were silent at first, Musk’s companies eventually apologized and claimed that additional safeguards were implemented and policies redesigned to block harmful outputs. However, state attorneys general alleged that those statements were “misleading” and that SpaceXSI instead quietly “embraced” sexualized content to seize more AI market share, as Grok continues to generate NCII and CSAM today.

Without intervention, kids in Virginia and Oregon risk a lifetime of distress, as Grok images will likely be impossible to remove online.

“Once created and shared,” Grok-generated CSAM and NCII “can never be fully erased, and it becomes a permanent record of the child’s abuse that may resurface for the rest of the child’s life,” Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones’ complaint remarked. “Virginia has a profound interest in protecting its children from this harm.”.

Sources indicate that millions of residents were allegedly harmed, as the attorneys general seek to protect every Grok or X user in their state. Many Grok victims will likely suffer from chronic anxiety, depression, and PTSD, as well as reputational harm, as some viewers may not realize the images are AI-generated, the states alleged. Further—due to Grok’s integration with the social media platform X—users as young as 13 may have been exposed to the AI content and possibly re-traumatized if they, too, are victims of sexual abuse, the states alleged.

“xAI not only knowingly endangered kids and our communities, but they also lied to our faces about non-existent safety measures,” Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield remarked in a press release.

It has been revealed that states alleged that xAI could have conducted rigorous red-teaming to block outputs before the fresh feature launched. But instead, the X Safety team responsible for Grok red-teaming was reduced to two or three team members, states alleged.

Overall, rather than use industry-standard safeguards, Musk’s firms allegedly put profits over women’s and children’s safety, states alleged, while complaining that SpaceXSI won’t even publicly identify “the officers responsible for safety governance.”.

In a recent development, “Industry standard requires not only building guardrails but also vigilantly monitoring whether they hold,” states alleged. SpaceXSI is doing neither effectively, states alleged.

Asked for comment, SpaceXSI shared an X Safety post on X, which repeated claims that the manufacturer has a “zero-tolerance” policy for “any forms of child sexual exploitation.” X Safety noted that the company “acted promptly to tighten” Grok protections, which are supposedly “designed to refuse any request to generate explicit images of minors or real people.” That statement also claimed that X Safety continually tests and adjusts protections when bad actors find ways to avoid filters, while relying on “sophisticated classifiers that screen every prompt” to catch harmful outputs “before an image is generated and check every output after.” Although the statement did not mention whether xAI sues people who break Grok rules to generate CSAM and NCII, it emphasized that xAI reports harmful content generated to police.

According to recent reports, “When someone tries to break our safeguards and generate this content, we take appropriate measures, including actioning accounts and notifying law enforcement,” X Safety said. “Attempting to create this material is a serious crime, and the individuals who do it should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law. We will continue to work with the authorities via all available means to pursue these bad actors.”.

However, state attorneys general alleged that reports from independent researchers and news outlets this year have shown that Grok is still generating NCII and CSAM. They noted that the chatbot “even advises people how to circumvent its own limited moderation measures to generate those images.” In some cases, a Virginia state probe found that Grok complied “with a user request to draft a prompt designed to avoid moderation.” So, even when filters work, the chatbot helps determined users immediately get around them, states alleged.

Sources indicate that nothing xAI did put a dent in the harmful outputs, least of all putting the feature behind a paywall, states alleged, which only ensured maximum profits. A troubled Newly introduced York City Council speaker, Julie Menin, confronted SpaceX this October with proof that attempts to digitally undress her own photo still worked for free Grok owners, states alleged.

Concluding its probe, Virginia found that moderation remains “inconsistent and ineffective,” with Grok sometimes carrying out prompts “that it later blocked.”.

In its complaint, Virginia alleged that Grok protections “were weak, ineffective, sparsely enforced, and easily circumvented.” Oregon agreed that rather than act to protect users, SpaceX entities repeatedly made statements “with the intent to deceive consumers” that Grok was safe. Most egregiously to state attorneys general, in January, Elon Musk denied any harm to real people, claiming that Grok is only “supposed [to] allow upper body nudity of imaginary adult humans (not real ones) and only generated nudity of fake people (not real ones).”.

“Contrary to Musk’s representation,” Grok “makes the same sexualizing edits to photographs of real, identifiable people,” states warned. “Defendants intentionally released a product that inundated their platforms with CSAM, NCII, and non-consensual sexualized images,” they alleged, and other “contemporaneous statements by Musk make clear that Grok’s ability to create sexualized material was part of xAI’s business strategy.”.

It’s also troubling to states that the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) reported to Congress that more than 90 percent of the Grok-generated CSAM that xAI submitted to its CyberTipline was considered a “dead end.”.

Industry observers note that as NCMEC explained, xAI initially refused to provide NCMEC and police with “basic user information, including location information, that law enforcement needs to act.” To fix the problem, NCMEC had to set up a meeting with xAI and get the reports resubmitted. This, states alleged, confirmed that “the information existed and that xAI had not provided it.” The concerning omission allegedly slowed down police response, just as the average number of Grok CSAM reports jumped by 88 percent from December 2025 to January 2026, then increased by another 66 percent from January to June 2026.

“X users were subjected to the risk that any person, at any time, could use their likeness to create CSAM, NCII, or other non-consensual sexualized images,” states alleged.

Lawmakers have asked state courts for an injunction blocking SpaceX entities from violating consumer protection laws by allegedly operating Grok without industry standard safeguards. If they win, they want SpaceX to pay thousands in civil penalties per violation, as well as disgorge any ill-gotten gains from marketing the chatbot as safe to people.

“Most people who use social media do not want to contribute to the harm caused to victims of CSAM, NCII, and other non-consensual sexualized images by being exposed to those images online,” states alleged.

Although Oregon’s complaint only vaguely estimates the number of people Grok attracted with Musk’s allegedly deceitful marketing strategy as at least “hundreds of thousands,” Virginia’s complaint included more detailed estimates. It said that approximately 6.4 million X accounts were linked to geolocations in the state, while the Grok application was downloaded 986,624 times by users with Virginia-based IP addresses.

“When xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it,” Jones remarked. “Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this firm accountable.”.

Is North Korea holding back on sending Russia more troops?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (780 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the summer, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy remarked that he expected between 30,000 and 50,000 North Korean soldiers would be deployed to Russia as part of Pyongyang's ongoing support of Moscow's war effort.
  • However, it now appears that troop buildup has yet to materialize, and it is unclear whether North Korea will continue sending large numbers of troops to Russia.
  • Writing on Telegram on November 9, Andrii Kovalenko, who resigned in September as head of Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation, said an August intelligence assessment indicated that the Kremlin had requested more than 30,000 additional North Korean troops for an autumn offensive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the summer, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy remarked that he expected between 30,000 and 50,000 North Korean soldiers would be deployed to Russia as part of Pyongyang's ongoing support of Moscow's war effort.

However, it now appears that troop buildup has yet to materialize, and it is unclear whether North Korea will continue sending large numbers of troops to Russia.

Writing on Telegram on November 9, Andrii Kovalenko, who resigned in September as head of Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation, said an August intelligence assessment indicated that the Kremlin had requested more than 30,000 additional North Korean troops for an autumn offensive.

He remarked a summit between North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and Russian President Vladimir Putin was expected in September, but did not happen. Kviy has claimed that North Korea previously sent thousands of troops to Russia's Kursk region in 2024, where Moscow was fighting to repel a Ukrainian incursion.

Kovalenko believes Pyongyang turned down Moscow's request because taking part in offensive operations in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine's Donetsk region may still be a red line for North Korea.

However, Kovalenko added that Russia still relies on North Korean material support, particularly ammunition, while assessing that another major deployment of North Korean combat troops was unlikely this winter.

Han Ki-bum, a former deputy director of South Korea's National Intelligence Service, told DW that the lull in fighting and the onset of winter give Pyongyang little immediate reason to send reinforcements.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

He added that a visit this week to Moscow by Jo Yong-won, a senior North Korean official and close aide to Kim, could shed light on any future plans.

Han stated it remained to be seen whether the visit was intended to deepen political ties between the ruling parties, building on their military cooperation, or to lay the groundwork for a visit by Kim himself.

Ahn Chan-il, a former North Korean soldier who defected to South Korea in 1979 and now heads the World Institute for North Korea Studies in Seoul, said Moscow also had reasons to limit the deployment.

He told DW that he expects Russia to weigh its battlefield needs against the costs of bringing in more North Korean troops. Unless the war expands, he noted, Moscow is unlikely to request a larger contingent.

Ukrainian official Kovalenko remarked North Korea still had a missile unit in Russia's Voronezh region and around 8,500 support personnel in rear areas, including drone operators, engineers and sappers.

He added that Pyongyang was ramping up ammunition production and showcasing newly introduced drones and missiles.

In a post on X on November 17, Zelenskyy stated that Russia was receiving dozens of North Korean ballistic missiles each month.

He warned that their use in Ukraine was helping Pyongyang refine its weapons and creating security risks for countries around the Korean Peninsula. Battle-testing weaponry is one of North Korea's primary advantages from military cooperation with Russia.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Kovalenko noted Pyongyang appeared to have adopted what he called a "containment strategy," limiting its military commitment to Russia's war while maintaining ties with both Moscow and Beijing.

In his assessment, this approach allows Pyongyang to retain the benefits of its alliance with Russia while reducing its exposure to the outcome of the war.

Analyst Ahn said he expects Pyongyang's military cooperation with Moscow to continue because Russian assistance is crucial to North Korea's efforts to develop drone technology and strengthen its navy.

Nevertheless, the extent of this cooperation may be more limited in the future, and Pyongyang is also able to turn to China as a hedge.

Ahn stated that if Russia limits the deployment of North Korean troops, Pyongyang's foreign currency earnings from those deployments would have less room to grow, giving it another reason to seek more support from Beijing.

Jeong Joon Hee, a former South Korean Unification Ministry spokesperson, told DW that recent moves towards building better ties with Beijing may also reflect Pyongyang's dissatisfaction with what Moscow has offered in return for North Korea's help.

By strengthening its relationship with China while keeping ties with Russia steady, he said, Pyongyang could also be trying to persuade Moscow to give it more.

According to recent reports, kim Hyung Suk, a former South Korean vice minister of unification, told DW that North Korea needs China's economic, political and diplomatic backing alongside the support it receives from Russia. He expects Pyongyang to keep pursuing China's support regardless of how it manages its role in the war.

Retail turnarounds are taking hold just in time for the holiday season

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Once-struggling retailers are entering the holiday quarter with improved performance and sales momentum as turnaround efforts begin to resonate with shoppers.
  • A handful of earnings reports on Tuesday pointed to a mix of factors behind the strong results, including a resilient consumer, stronger execution and demand for the right products at the right price.
  • Recent findings suggest that kohl's reported comparable sales growth of 1.2% for the period ended Oct.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Once-struggling retailers are entering the holiday quarter with improved performance and sales momentum as turnaround efforts begin to resonate with shoppers.

A handful of earnings reports on Tuesday pointed to a mix of factors behind the strong results, including a resilient consumer, stronger execution and demand for the right products at the right price.

Recent findings suggest that kohl's reported comparable sales growth of 1.2% for the period ended Oct. 31 and raised its full-year outlook as CEO Michael Bender said customers "have remained resilient" but are "migrating to value with their purchases.".

He tied improvement to the company's work on product assortment, store experience and value.

Best Buy also on Tuesday posted its highest comparable sales growth in five years, at 6.1%, which prompted the electronics retailer to raise its full-year outlook.

"We have a tremendous amount of momentum," CEO Jason Bonfig told CNBC in an interview. "The fact that we saw pretty much broad-based growth across almost all of our categories is a lot of momentum that we're very excited about.".

The company also credited execution, market share gains and a compelling product cycle alongside growing customer demand.

At Dick's Sporting Goods, quarterly comparable sales rose 2.6% at the core business and 0.5% at Foot Locker. CEO Lauren Hobart mentioned "all income demographics grew" and the company "didn't see trade-down from best to better or better to good.".

Industry observers note that she similarly pointed to latest products and market share gains within the category as contributing to the strong quarter. She also highlighted continued improvement at Foot Locker.

All three companies have been undergoing efforts to boost sales and get the right products on shelves to meet customer demand.

Target, likewise undergoing revitalization efforts, last week reported comparable sales growth of 5.6% in the third quarter, fueled by a 5% increase in comparable traffic. The retailer raised its full-year outlook.

CEO Michael Fiddelke at the time called the traffic gain "a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often.".

Even Gap CEO Richard Dickson told CNBC the organization has moved from "rebuild mode" to "turnaround mode" at its Old Navy banner, a sign of progress, albeit not a broad-based portfolio recovery.

Sources indicate that michael Baker, a retail analyst at D.A. Davidson, told CNBC he sees both a resilient consumer and organization-specific improvements as driving sector strength.

In a recent development, "Retail sales have been more resilient than most think," Baker remarked. His analysis revealed retail sales, excluding autos and gas, rose 5.1% in the third quarter on a nonseasonally adjusted basis — the strongest quarter since the pandemic.

But he cautioned that growth appears to be coming more from transaction size than traffic, with inflation, promotions and higher units per transaction driving up spend.

It has been revealed that dollar Tree, which reported better-than-expected earnings on Tuesday morning, posted a 3.8% increase to traffic, accelerating from 0.4% growth in the prior quarter, suggesting more shoppers may be bargain hunting. Comparable sales at the retailer increased 4.6% during the period.

It has been revealed that "Consumers are under pressure, and they are increasingly selective about where and how they spend," mentioned Dollar Tree CEO Michael Creedon on the organization's earnings call. "When under pressure, shoppers prioritize value and buy closer to need.".

Comparable sales of everyday essentials rose 8.9% at Dollar Tree stores in the third quarter, while sales of nonessential items were essentially flat, the tech giant stated.

— CNBC's Laya Neelakandan contributed to this report.

Trump halts Iowa detonation, indicates fresh governor to blame if it blows accidentally

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (842 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Trump took to social media Monday afternoon to announce that he has ordered the US military to halt looks to detonate 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide at an Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa.
  • Sources indicate that the Army had planned to detonate the barrels on November 20, but delayed the blast on Thursday amid public outcry and a legal challenge from environmental groups.
  • Iowa residents and officials said they learned of the detonation only days beforehand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Trump took to social media Monday afternoon to announce that he has ordered the US military to halt looks to detonate 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide at an Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. Trump claimed that the fate of the unstable, highly explosive material is now in the hands of a federal court and Rob Sand, Iowa’s governor-elect, who won’t be sworn into office until January.

Sources indicate that the Army had planned to detonate the barrels on November 20, but delayed the blast on Thursday amid public outcry and a legal challenge from environmental groups. The explosion will launch a plume of toxic gases and neurotoxic lead that could reach up to 100 miles away from the Iowa facility, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP).

Iowa residents and officials said they learned of the detonation only days beforehand. The environmental groups, led by Earthjustice, claimed in an emergency court filing that the Army had not fully considered safer options for disposing of the lead azide before planning the detonation.

It has been revealed that late Thursday, a federal appeals court granted Earthjustice’s request to put a hold on the Army’s permit from the Environmental Protection Agency, which allowed for the controlled detonation to be carried out. Around the same time, Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle mentioned the detonation would be postponed until Monday so the military could communicate with Iowans about the situation and looks.

Documents released by the Army last week mentioned that the military first learned in March that the lead azide had started to degrade and crystallize. Lead azide is used in detonators for munitions, but in crystallized form it becomes highly unstable and sensitive to physical movement or friction. The IAAAP is said to contain around 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of lead azide in barrels held in earth-covered containers.

Sources indicate that in late March, the Army awarded a contract to MuniRem Environmental, a Georgia-based firm that uses chemicals to neutralize munitions to safely dispose of the lead azide, according to a New York Times report. MuniRem uses a sulfur-based solution that reportedly breaks down explosives and immobilizes toxic chemicals, eliminating the need for detonation. The company had proposed spraying the inside of the earth-covered containers housing the barrels as well as the barrel surfaces to neutralize risks of spontaneous explosions.

Sources indicate that but two months later, the Army canceled the contract without explanation. An Army contracting officer told MuniRem in an email at the time that the cancellation “was not based on deficiencies” in MuniRem’s plans, the Times reported. The firm’s founder said MuniRem filed public records requests to get more information on why the contract was scrapped, but it has not received a response.

According to recent reports, now, the Army claims that the lead azide has only degraded further since March and that it cannot move the barrels or even open their lids without risking a catastrophic explosion. Further, it claims that winter temperatures in the coming days increase the risk of spontaneous detonation.

“As the temperatures drop, the risk of an uncontrolled explosion increases because the formed crystals can break more easily in freezing temperatures,” lawyers for the Trump administration wrote in a court filing over the weekend. “If the crystals break, this could cause a chain reaction detonation that could cause an uncontrolled dispersal of lead azide into the environment.”.

The Army claims that the only choice now is between a controlled, mitigated explosion or an uncontrolled, unmitigated explosion. In court filings this weekend, government lawyers argued that the Army does not need the now-suspended EPA permit to move forward with the detonation, because the Army has determined that the lead azide poses an “immediate threat to human health, public safety, property, or the environment.”.

According to recent reports, last Thursday, Telle remarked that the delay until Monday was the “latest possible moment” for a controlled detonation before temperatures dropped dangerously low. But the military subsequently delayed the detonation again until Tuesday and then pushed it back to Wednesday.

Sources indicate that in his social media post Monday, Trump noted he thought carrying out the controlled detonation was the “proper course.” But he said he was making the decision the responsibility of the federal appeals court and Governor-elect Rob Sand, a Democrat. If the lead azide spontaneously detonates on their watch, Trump claimed, they will be fully to blame.

“If he or the Courts do not agree, we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation,” Trump wrote.

In a social media post Sunday evening, Sand called for answers on how the situation was able to become so dangerous, specifically raising the question of why MuniRem’s contract was canceled.

“Iowans deserve transparency over how we got here, then answers and accountability to stop this from ever happening again,” he wrote.

Just imagine you're an actor who booked an unspecified gig years ago and then found out nearly half a decade later that you were performing a role in the biggest video game of all time, Grand Theft Auto VI?

Recent findings suggest that pretty cool, huh? That's exactly what happened to 63-year-old Guy A. Fortt.

Sources indicate that and if you were Fortt, you'd probably want to proudly show off your scenes to your whole family and all of your friends. Right? There's one massive problem for Fortt, though: He has no idea who he played in GTA 6.

Sources indicate that and there's another matter for Fortt, who, according to IGN, previously had roles in both Jessica Jones and The Sopranos. He doesn't have an Xbox or PlayStation 5, so he can't even play the game and try to find his character(s).

However, Fortt does have a Facebook and Instagram account. And he posted a video on both detailing his GTA 6 dilemma. Now, according to Fortt in a follow-up video, millions of gamers are essentially on an in-game scavenger hunt to find the character or characters that Fortt played.

It has been revealed that "I was a motion capture actor on GTA 6, but I don't know who the hell I am,” Fortt explained in his viral Instagram video. "I auditioned about four or five years ago; they put the balls all over my body and face. And then I forgot all about it." #105337. Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1186 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Technologyreview ↗ Open Full Page

Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1186 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that one of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade.
  • xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024.
  • As of October 2026, data center developers have announced prepares for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that one of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles. But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.

As of October 2026, data center developers have announced prepares for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.

It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.

Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” indicates Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.

It has been revealed that when developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.

Sources indicate that rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some crucial questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” indicates Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.

Sources indicate that behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont notes.

Industry observers note that even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.

The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.).

Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.

In a recent development, today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi states. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.

BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report. That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.

According to recent reports, and while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, states Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices.

There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data.

Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.

While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study, his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels.

Industry observers note that “These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp states. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Land mines killed or injured more people in 2025 than in any year since 2020, according to the International Campaign to Ban Landmines' (ICBL) annual report.
    • The report stated that the number of recorded deaths was at least 6,929, which is a 10% increase compared with last year.
    • Experts say the true figure is likely higher as not all land mine related death and injuries are recorded as such.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Land mines killed or injured more people in 2025 than in any year since 2020, according to the International Campaign to Ban Landmines' (ICBL) annual report.

    The report stated that the number of recorded deaths was at least 6,929, which is a 10% increase compared with last year. According to the campaign, four out of five victims were civilians, and half of those were minors.

    Experts say the true figure is likely higher as not all land mine related death and injuries are recorded as such.

    Myanmar reported the highest annual casualty toll for the third year in a row, with 1,891 victims, amid a "massive" new mine use.

    In Syria, the number of casualties climbed by 50% to 1,602 in 2025, after the large-scale return of displaced people following the ousting of president Bashar Assad.

    Myanmar and Syria were followed by Afghanistan with 497 casualties.

    Recent findings suggest that the ICBL criticized Ukraine, over its continued use of land mines. Ukraine, which is presently being invaded by Russia, is one of the 162 state parties to the Mine Ban Treaty.

    It has been revealed that the treaty, known as the Ottawa Treaty, prohibits the use, production, storage and transfer of anti-personnel mines. The treaty was ratified by 166 countries, but not by China, India, Russia, Israel, North Korea, or the US, along with nearly 30 others.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Industry observers note that five European NATO countries, which share a border with Russia, have withdrawn from the treaty last year: Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Finland and Poland. Ukraine has also withdrawn, though this will not take legal effect until the war ends.

    "The treaty’s norms face their greatest test since 1999," the report said, citing the withdrawals.

    In 2025, Ukraine justified its move to withdraw from the treaty by citing the actions of Russia, which has never ratified the treaty and has been using mines on Ukrainian territory.

    According to recent reports, the campaign said Ukraine was still "fully bound by the treaty" but had breached its ban on producing anti-personnel mines. It said the country had manufactured both 3D-printed mines and mines designed to be dropped by drones.

    Report also noted that Russia has used antipersonnel land mines extensively in Ukraine since its full-scale invasion began in 2022.

    Afghanistan, Azerbaijan, Cambodia, Iraq, Morocco, North Korea, South Korea and Ukraine have "massive land mine contamination," meaning they have more than 100 square kilometers of land contaminated by land mines, the report assessed.

    Since 1999, 49,859 people were killed and 118,525 injured by land mines, according to Landmine and Cluster Munition Monitor, the research and monitoring arm of the ICBL, and the Cluster Munition Coalition NGOs.

    Industry News: 11 Things Jensen Huang Actually Said at His First All-Hands Back at Nvidia

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (691 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Jensen Huang is going to therapy for 90 minutes a day and rethinking his management style, and he states that violating Nvidia’s code of conduct isn’t necessarily a fireable offense.
    • In a recent development, here are some of the most striking things Huang said during the meeting, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED.
    • It has been revealed that on self-improvement: “I go to therapy every day for an hour and a half.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Jensen Huang is going to therapy for 90 minutes a day and rethinking his management style, and he states that violating Nvidia’s code of conduct isn’t necessarily a fireable offense. That’s just some of what the newly returned Nvidia CEO told staff during his first all-hands meeting on Tuesday.

    In a recent development, here are some of the most striking things Huang said during the meeting, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

    It has been revealed that on self-improvement: “I go to therapy every day for an hour and a half. And it’s been helping me a lot.”.

    It has been revealed that on accountability: “There are rumors on the internet that apparently I’m a tech bro, and therefore I’m back. Apparently, I’m a tech bro, and because I wear a super nice jacket, that I’m above the law, and I’m above the code of conduct. That is not true. It won’t be tolerated, and it wasn’t tolerated here.”.

    “If one of you were to violate a code of conduct, what does that mean? If you were ever to violate a code of conduct, it is not appropriate. I just wanted you to know, it is not right, it's not appropriate, it won’t be tolerated. But ‘it won’t be tolerated’ does not mean the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door. Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments. And your management team will still make the decision. That is what is in the best interest of the firm and its employees, with all the facts and circumstances.”.

    On his management style: “The intensity I bring elevates everybody else. But I can go too far. When I go too far, it hurts people, it belittles them, it disempowers them. And that’s not right. And so I need to go figure out how I’m going to bring the intensity, the crazy intensity, to the field.”.

    On women at Nvidia: “I believe we need to create and continue to sustain a safe environment for all of our women. And if I did anything that put that in jeopardy, I cannot tell you how sad I am, and I’ll do everything I can to fix it. We will not tolerate that.”.

    According to recent reports, on succession: “All day long, this company can run autonomously, and you saw it. I promise you, whether I’m here or not, this company is wired up to execute, execute, and execute, and deliver on financial results.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “I also didn’t believe in succession planning. Let that sink in. I don’t believe in succession planning. I think it’s flawed. The idea of succession planning is not flawed. What people think succession planning means is flawed.”.

    It has been revealed that “There’s a reason why we don’t have succession planning; it’s not because we are unaware of the word. I’m the longest-running tech CEO in history.”.

    On politics: “There [were] also rumors that apparently I’m back because the highest levels of our government wanted me back. That is also completely untrue. Our board of directors performed their duty as they should have.”.

    Sources indicate that “It is absolutely true that President Trump really, really loves our tech giant,” Huang told employees. “He gloats about Nvidia. You know he does. But there’s a question about politics. Are we now political? Are we partisan? I wanna be very clear with you. President Trump is the United States president. He is my president. And I’ll do everything I can to help this president be informed about how he could make decisions that are in the best interest of our country … We have to do it, and whoever the next president is will be my president, and I will do exactly the same.”.

    According to recent reports, “Don’t think for a second that politics ever plays a role in this organization, not even a little bit. We are the most apolitical company. I don’t love that we talk about politics here. Take it home. I love that we talk about work here.”.

    • Industry observers note that zelenskyy noted that a Ka-27 combat helicopter onboard the Merkury was also destroyed.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ukrainian explosive naval drones sank a Russian warship docked in the port city of Benghazi in Libya while also striking a Russian cargo ship that it was escorting. The incident demonstrates the expanding scope of Ukrainian military strikes on Russian ships from the coast of North Africa to the Gulf of Finland.

    The Russian Navy’s missile corvette Merkury sank at port after being struck by at least two Ukrainian naval drones on November 22, according to The Associated Press. Ukraine’s Security Service described using seven naval drones introduced from a mother ship to target the Merkury, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy shared video footage showing the drone boats approaching and exploding against both the burning Russian warship and a Russian dry cargo ship, MV Angara.

    Industry observers note that zelenskyy noted that a Ka-27 combat helicopter onboard the Merkury was also destroyed. He described the cargo ship MV Angara as transporting weapons—Russia provides material support to the Libyan National Army that at the moment controls Benghazi and is battling the internationally recognized Libyan government based in Tripoli.

    Casualties from the strikes included at least 10 people, including Libyan and Russian nationals, Libyan National Army officials told The Associated Press. They also mentioned some wounded crew members of the Russian warship being transferred to local hospitals.

    Industry observers note that merkury was a Steregushchiy-class missile corvette, designated by Russia as Project 20380, that can carry both anti-ship and air-defense missiles. They are also armed with torpedoes to counter submarines and have a naval cannon mounted on the deck.

    Corvette-class warships are typically smaller than the destroyers or frigates that often act as workhorses of modern navies, although NATO has designated Russian missile corvettes such as the Merkury as being equivalent to frigates.

    Merkury was originally meant to join Russia’s Black Sea Fleet. But after Russia released its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the Russian warship was unable to enter the Black Sea because Turkey invoked the 1936 Montreux Convention to restrict warships from entering or leaving the Black Sea. Instead, the Merkury mainly operated from Russia’s Northern Fleet bases in Arctic waters, according to naval analyst HI Sutton.

    In a recent development, the sinking of the Merkury marks the latest significant setback for the Russian Navy, which nominally remains one of the world’s leading navies in terms of number of ships and capability. The attack also reveals Ukraine’s expanding geographical deployment of sea drones, which resemble low-profile drone boats that can be armed with machine guns, missiles, and explosives when engaged in kamikaze ramming missions.

    Recent findings suggest that ukraine has used such drone boats in combination with flying drones and missiles to challenge the Russian Navy’s control of the Black Sea and Sea of Azov, which hold crucial shipping lanes for both countries and represent staging grounds for military operations. Ukraine has struck Russian warships at sea and in port, including another Russian missile corvette named the Boikiy that was seriously damaged by Ukrainian aerial drones while docked in St. Petersburg in June, according to Naval News.

    Ukraine’s contestation of the Black Sea also undermines Russian efforts to maintain control of the Crimean Peninsula, which Russian forces seized from Ukraine in 2014. For example, Ukrainian aerial drone strikes on dozens of Russian-linked tankers and cargo ships in the Sea of Azov in July 2026 forced Russia to severely restrict resupply runs by sea.

    Throughout 2026, Ukraine has also steadily increased its mid-range drone strike campaign targeting Russian roads and railways along the limited land-based supply corridors connecting Russia to Crimea.

    On the nights of November 15 and November 16, waves of Ukrainian drones and missiles succeeded in collapsing one of two steel arches supporting the Kerch Strait Bridge—a structure built by Russian President Vladimir Putin’s regime as both a symbolic and physical link between Russia and Crimea.

    That has left only the bridge’s railway still functional as a supply link for Russian-occupied Crimea, although Ukraine has continued targeting the remaining structure. Fallen debris from the bridge’s steel arch and roadway has also blocked the only deep-water route that allowed ships to pass through the Kerch Strait between the Sea of Azov and Black Sea.

    But Russia has struck back with its own drone and missile strikes on Ukrainian ports and third-party ships traveling to and from Ukrainian ports. Starting in October, Russian aerial and sea drones also began striking and sinking commercial shipping near the coasts of NATO member countries Bulgaria and Romania.

    Meanwhile, Ukraine has increasingly taken the fight against Russia beyond the Black Sea. Ukraine’s sinking of the Merkury and strike on the MV Angara are only the latest examples of such strikes in the Mediterranean Sea.

    In a recent development, the most notable previous example involved the liquefied natural gas tanker Arctic Metagaz—a shadow fleet ship sanctioned for carrying Russian oil—that was wrecked by massive explosions while heading for Benghazi on March 3. Russia described the ship as having been struck by Ukrainian sea drones in the Mediterranean, although Ukraine did not publicly take credit for the attack, according to The Guardian.

    According to recent reports, more recently, Ukraine has also expanded its drone strikes northward to Russian-linked ships in the Gulf of Finland within the Baltic Sea. On November 11, Finnish authorities confirmed a strike on a Russian Navy Buyan-M class corvette named Naro-Fominsk, with Ukraine’s Security Service later claiming credit, according to BBC News. The damaged warship headed back to the Russian port of St. Petersburg.

    Recent findings suggest that that incident was followed by at least two drone strikes on the Russian dry cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland on November 21, according to ERR News. The Sparta II is sanctioned by the United States and described by Ukraine as a Russian ship that has carried weapons and military equipment in the past.

    According to recent reports, finnish authorities coordinated the rescue and response effort that also included Russian and Estonian ships, with the Sparta II eventually being towed by a Russian ship back to St. Petersburg, Reuters reported. But in a social media post, Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo also described the situation as follows: “Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”.

    Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose

    📅 04 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1368 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China debuted last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.
    • At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.
    • It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China debuted last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

    At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

    It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

    This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

    It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

    A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

    But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

    “This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

    That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

    The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

    “Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun noted. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

    The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

    Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

    Sources indicate that taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

    But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

    For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to newly introduced heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he remarked.

    That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

    China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

    According to recent reports, china thinks it's diplomatically isolating Taiwan. It isn't.

    The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

    That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”.

    It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

    Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

    While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

    Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

    Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

    Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

    A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

    Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

    This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

    But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

    As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

    It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

    Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

    What you need to know about China-Taiwan tensions.

    Industry observers note that china is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

    Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

    This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an crucial opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

    An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

    “(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” stated Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

    “A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”.

    CNN’s Wayne Chang contributed reporting.
